items.text: Fiftieth Parliament
Parliamentary Debates
(HANSARD)
Tuesday, 28 January 2014
(for inclusion in Volume 696)
Published under the authority of the House of Representatives—2014
TUESDAY, 28 JANUARY 2014
RESIGNATIONS—
BY-ELECTION—
MOTIONS—
POINTS OF ORDER—
SUBANTARCTIC ISLANDS MARINE RESERVES BILL—
ACCOUNTING INFRASTRUCTURE REFORM BILL—
ARTS COUNCIL OF NEW ZEALAND TOI AOTEAROA BILL—
28 Jan 2014 Resignations 15521

Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
Katrina Shanks, New Zealand National

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I wish to advise the House that I have received a letter from Katrina
Shanks, resigning her seat with effect from Tuesday, 21 January 2014.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received from the Elector al Commission a return declaring
Joanne Kowhai Hayes to be elected a member of Parliament to fill the vacancy created
by the resignation of Katrina Shanks.
Christchurch East

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received from the Electoral Commission a writ declaring
Munokoa Poto Williams to be elected to repres ent the electorate of Christchurch East. I
understand that Poto Williams is present and wishes to make the affirmation. Would she
please come forward to the chair on my right.
Poto Williams was presented to the Speaker, made the affirmation required by law,
and took her seat in the House.
Mr Speaker administered the Oath of Allegiance to Joanne Hayes, who then took her
seat in the House.
MOTIONS
Lorde—Grammy Awards Success

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion without
notice congratulating Lorde on her success at the Grammy Awards.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That this House congratul ate Ella Yelich-O’Connor,
also known as Lorde, on her success at the 56 th annual Grammy Awards . Yesterday
young New Zealander Ella Yelich-O’Connor  made history. Th e singer-songwriter
known as Lorde won the Grammy for best pop solo performance and together with co-
producer Joel Little won song of the year  for “Royals”. She was nominated for an
unbelievable four Grammys.
Rolling Stone has called Lorde pop’s most unlikely new superstar, and for very good
reason. She has just achieved something no New Zealander has, and that it has
happened so quickly and so comprehensivel y has taken the world by surprise. In less
than a year Lorde has gone from being a year-12 student at Takapuna Grammar School
to superstardom. Her unique brand of alterna tive pop has seen her top charts not just in
New Zealand but in Britain, Australia, Belg ium, Ireland, and Canada. She has appeared
on the Letterman show and on Ellen, and exchanges text me ssages these days with
Taylor Swift.
She is just 17 years old, but what is most remarkable about Ella is that she has done it
all in her own way—a typically Kiwi and unassuming way. If there were rules, no one
15522 Motions 28 Jan 2014
told Lorde. She has busted stereotypes and, along the way, won hearts. Her performance
at yesterday’s Grammys earned her a sta nding ovation—think about  that, a standing
ovation—from the most influential names in the history of music.
New Zealand is a nation of high achiev ers. We almost always punch above our
weight. However, the success of Ella Yeli ch-O’Connor is remarkable even by those
standards. Yesterday this talented young woman make New Zealand sit up and take
notice. I suspect there will be many such moments as her career goes forward. Ella and
Joel, you have made New Zealand very proud.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Labour today congratulates
young New Zealand musician Ella Yelich- O’Connor, aka Lorde, on her Grammy
success yesterday. All New Zealanders are proud of Ella’s achievements, her lyrics, and
what she stands for, which resonates w ith all young New Zealanders—young musicians
striving to achieve their dreams. Ella is a role model for all New Zealanders and New

items.speaker: Zealand musicians. Lorde has won two Grammy s
items.text: one for Song of the Year for her hit
“Royals” and one for Best Pop Solo Performance. Lorde was nominated amongst big
names in the music business, including Bruno Mars, Katy Perry, Macklemore, and
others. Past winners of Song of the Year include Adele for her 2011 hit “Rolling in the
Deep”.
Many musicians have praised the young New Zealander nationally and
internationally for her amazing achieveme nts, and she now joins a long list of
worldwide music legends. She joins the most recent New Zealand Grammy winner
Kimbra, who last year won Record of th e Year and Best Pop Duo/Group Performance
with Australian musician Gotye for “Somebody That I Used to Know”.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: The Green Party joins with this
Parliament and with the rest of the country  in congratulating Ella Yelich-O’Connor and
Joel Little on their amazing success at the Grammys. It was a very proud moment and
there were thousands and thousands of Ne w Zealanders amongst the 30 million other
people around the world watching this young New Zealand woman and this young New
Zealand man take the stage and take the world by storm in this amazing event. It is all
about their passion and their creativity and their hard work, which led them there, along
with the support of their families and their friends and the creative community that sits
around them. How amazing it is to see this young, 17-year-old woma n meet all of her
talent and fulfil all of her potential, and how amazing it would be if we could be assured
that every single New Zealand child had everything they needed, too, to meet all of their
potential, to fulfil all their talents, and to achieve on the world stage or at home in the
best way that they can. She is a fantastic example of what can be achieved by our young
people if they have the support that they need.
I am also really pleased that the s ong itself was the one that won best song—
“Royals”—because this song was all about how we do not need all of that crazy wealth
or all of that crazy greed. Actually, it is enough to have friends and family and to do
amazing things, to have your talent and your pot ential fulfilled. What a great thing that
is—[Interruption] Absolutely—let us clap that. And let us clap a young woman who
was able to write about that and to express that to the world in such an amazing way.
We are very proud of this young woman and everyone who supports her. Thank you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: New Zealand First wishes to
join other political parties in offering our congratulations to both Ella and Joel on their
stunning success. I want to also say that we do not seek any vicari ous benefit in this
parade today. So, suffice for us to say, on be half of New Zealand First, we are very
proud of you.
28 Jan 2014 Motions 15523

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: He mihi tuatahi, ng ā mihi
o te Tau Hou ki a koe, otir ā, ki a t ātau. Ko t ā te P āti Māori, he tautoko i ng ā kōrero ki
tēnei o ngā wāhine i whakanuia inapō nei. Ā, ka nui te mihi ki a ia.
[First of all, greetings of the New Year to you, Mr Speaker, and, indeed, to us. The
Māori Party endorses the statements made  to this among th e women who were
honoured last evening and acknowledge her greatly.]
I stand on behalf of the M āori Party to support other comments that have been made
about Lorde and Mr Joel Little and congrat ulate them on their win. Maybe there is
something to be said about changing your name to get that ultimate success, and I
suppose I have got to say for myself that something like “Jimbo” or “James” or
something like that might be a good idea in the future. I have got to say that Beyoncé
still does it for me, but Lorde is still right up there—Lorde is up there.
I understand that Dame Kiri Te Kanawa back in 1984 won the first Grammy awarded
to a New Zealander, and so Lorde has join ed a long queue of other people already
mentioned today whom we must acknowledge as bringing pride not only to themselves
and their families but also to the country. We  have got to think about their parents as
well, who have been mentione d, and say that o bviously that talent must come from
somewhere, and we acknowledge Lorde’s parents.
I understand that as a young person in 2009 at Belmont Intermediate, Lorde won
with a song called “Warwick Avenue”. I do not know the song—it wa s a little bit after
my time—but apparently that video was shown to Universal Music Group
representatives and, of course, subsequently they signed her to that label. Five years
later, of course with the support of her fa mily, those around her, her school, and with
her music—and I understand that she went ba ck to her school not long ago—she has
clearly demonstrated that she has the talent , and, according to most commentators, will
carry on with that success.
The last word, I think, would probably need to go back to her. In her first interview,
not even 1 year ago, she admitted to the success of her song-writing style as this:
“You’ve got to be honest for it to lock with me. It’s got to have real things …”. We love
the fact that she keeps it real and writes about  real things that are important to her, and
possibly touches the hearts and minds of ma ny people. Clearly, it does. We wish her
well.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Huri rauna, t ēnā
tātou katoa e hui tuatahi i tēnei rā roto i tō tātou Pāremata, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou. Me
te mihi anōki ki a tātou katoa kua tae mai, horekau he painga e pā ana ki tētahi i tēnei rā,
tēnā koutou, kia ora t ātou. Me mihi anōki au ki tērā o wā tātou nei kōtiro, a Lorde, i tae
atu ki te taumata o t ōna waiata. Ēngari, e tika ana kia kaua e wareware ki ng ā wāhine
rongonui o roto o Aotearoa, e noho tonu nei ki roto i a t ātou, i tae atu ki t ērā o ngā hui
whakangau o Ngāpuhi, e tū ana ki roto i a mātou i te wikiene kua pahure ake nei. Tetahi
ko Maisey Rika, ko Whirimako Black, ko Ri a Hall, Billie Anne Monga me taku k ōtiro
anōki a Magic. E tika ana kia mihi atu ki a r ātou e w’akarangatira ana i ng ā kaupapa
waiata o roto i a t ātou i tēnei wā. Mihi atu ki a Lorde, mihi atu ki a r ātou, mihi atu ki a
tātou. Tēnā koutou, kia ora tātou katoa.
Thank you, Mr Speaker. Greetings to us al l throughout, who are meeting for the first
time today in our Parliament, greetings. I acknowledge us all, as well, who have
nothing but goodwill for each other today, so  greetings and well done. I also pay a
tribute to Lorde, that one of our girls w hose song has reached its pinnacle. But it is
right that well-known women entertainers in  New Zealand who are living here still in
our midst are not overlooked. They arrived  in the weekend just past at one of the
festivals held amongst us in Ng āpuhi. One was Maisey Rika. Others were Whirimako
Black, Ria Hall, Billie Anne Monga, and my daught er Magic as well. It  is fitting that
15524 Motions 28 Jan 2014
they are acknowledged for promoting the songs being sung amongst us today. In
congratulating Lorde, I congratulate them too and us. Salutations and congratulations
to us all.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: What an extraordinary achievement for a
young New Zealander. Lorde has brought great cr edit to herself, her family, Takapuna
Grammar School, and the country. On behalf of  the people of Epsom, I join with the
Prime Minister in publicly congratulating her, her family, her supporters, and her
friends.
My bench mates suggested that on this occasion I should try to be very cool and
hook up with the young people listening to this br oadcast this afternoon. I am sure that
there are tens of thousands of young people tuned in to their crystal sets and hanging off
of every word we are saying about this great New Zealander.
This award represents a family who have  given her unconditional love and a world-
class education and taught her the value of hard work. It also represents her—obviously
inherited and worked—huge talent and ability, much confidence, and a brilliant future. I
was reflecting while my colleagues were speaking that, now that she is famous, if she is
thinking of coming to Parliament, do not. St ay with your day job. She can bring much,
much more credit to New Zealand than comi ng here. It is her sh eer genius that has
brought her to where she is, and she has much more ability to come and many more
accolades to arrive. I congratulate her and her family on this great award.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I doubt that there are many
people in New Zealand, or anywhere else in the world for that matter, who were
watching yesterday who did not become filled with emotion at watching this
extraordinary spectacle of th is delightfully natu ral, talented, effervescent young New
Zealander steal the show both with her rendition of her song at the beginning and then
with her genuine, unvarnished, natural remark s at the time when  she received her
awards. She was a reflection of all that we would like to think is good about young New

items.speaker: Zealanders
items.text: confident, assured, certain, bu t also natural, unaffected, and charming.
Lorde displayed all of those talents yesterda y. But yesterday is but a step along the way
in what will obviously be an extremely successful career.
Her achievements to date in  getting to this point s hould not be overlooked. Her
passion, her skill as a songwriter and a performer, and the chemistry that she exudes that
attracts people to watch her performances are all part of an extraordinary gift and an
extraordinary talent. Lorde, her family, he r supporters, her workmates, and her team
around her can all take extraordinary satisf action from her achievements to date. And
we as a country can be proud of her, not just  for the representation that she gives us but
for the fact that she shows the world what a good young New Zealander can be like. She
is a remarkable ambassadress, an extraord inary songstress and writer, and she is a
person we should be very, very proud to celebrate and acknowledge long into the future.
Motion agreed to.
Tabling of Documents—War Pensions

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek
leave of the House to table a letter to this Parliament from Viet Nam veteran John
“Doc” Mountain on behalf of many New Zeala nd services veterans, some of whom are
here today in this House, expressing grave concerns in the way wa r pensions, disabled
pensions—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is enough information for the House. I put leave to the
House. Leave is sought to table that particular document. [Interruption]
28 Jan 2014 Points of Order 15525

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I am seeking leave to speak to the point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think that on this particular occas ion it is useful for the Leader of
the House to seek clarification.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Mr Speaker, we have
arrangements in this House, as you we ll know, through the Business Committee, where
matters like this are often put in front of parties prior to their being brought to the
House. I do think that in this  case it would be better if the member were prepared to put
that to the Business Committee today to see what might come of it tomorrow, rather
than putting the House in a position of having to decline something it has not seen.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: With respect, it has crept in of
late that the Business Committee seems to be controlling events that really belong with
this House. The plain fact is that my co lleague has sought the House’s permission to
table a document. I cannot believe that there is any responsible member of Parliament
who would oppose him doing so.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member for his co ntribution. The Business Committee
works to smooth the running of this House. Mr Brownlee is quite right to suggest that in
the normal course of events such a matter as this would be ra ised through it. I think it is
now in the hands of the mover of the moti on, Andrew Williams. He is in the situation
where he withdraws it or I put the leave as he has requested. It is either of those two
choices. Can I seek clarification from Mr W illiams. Does he want to proceed with me
putting the question of leave?

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Mr Speaker, we have veterans here in the
House today—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I take it from that that the member wants me to proceed with
putting the question of leave. I therefore put the question. Leave is sought for that letter
to be tabled. Is there any objection? There is objection.
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move that this  House express its
confidence in the National-led Government—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I first of all ask the Prime Minister to present the Prime
Minister’s statement.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: He’s a first timer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Quite the opposite. Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Simply present the—

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I present the Prime Minister’s statement.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That paper is published under the authority of the House. Copies are
available on the Table. I call on Government order of the day—[ Interruption] Order! I
know everybody is very keen to get this year under way, no more so than myself.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Yay!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, thank you for the applause because I move, That this
House express its confidence in the National-led Government and commend its
programme for 2014 as set out in the Prime Minister’s statement.  This Government
starts the year where it left off: with a plan for New Zealand that we present today; with
a sense of what is required for economic management—affordable, sensible, and
responsible; with a vision for this great country; and with a united, dedicated, and
committed team.
The Opposition begins the year where it left  off: desperate, divided, and delusional.
Mercifully it was quite quiet over Christmas,  I have to say. David Cunliffe was very
15526 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
much like a white tiger: he was out there but no one actually ever saw him. Russel
Norman spent his entire summer break working out how he could get an invitation to go
back to the Dotcom mansion for the third time. Hone Harawira took a public tour of
Parliament to see what it is actually like. One thing that did ha ppen over Christmas,
though, was that the Opposition proved, I think quite clearly, that it should have gone to
summer school when it comes to mathema tics or economics, because it is quite one
thing when the Green Party wants to print m oney, but David Cunliffe has actually taken
that to a whole new level. You see, he has gone right past the prin ting press, right past
bitcoin, and he has now gone into imaginary or make-believe money. It is fantastic
stuff. You do not have to borrow it. You do not  have to print it. Y ou most certainly do
not have to earn it. According to David Cun liffe, all you have to do is spend it. That
takes you into that kind of interesting space of where the Opposition is these days.
As John Armstrong quite righ tly pointed out in the New Zealand Herald this
morning, it is a bit of a tricky Opposition. You need to actually read the fine print. This
is the Opposition that last year wanted New Z ealanders to believe that if they earned
under $18.40 an hour, they would get a pay ri se under Labour. But it  turns out in the
fine print that it is actually only if you are working for a Government department pretty
much in Wellington. He wanted them to belie ve that there was $1.5 billion just sitting
out there mysteriously waiting to be spent.  Yesterday he wanted  New Zealanders to
believe that if for an entire year they had a 1-year-old or younger and they earn under
$150,000 a year—Labour’s new definition of poverty—they would get 60 bucks a
week. But actually when you read the fine prin t, they do not. They get it after the paid
parental leave has finished. That is right. The Opposition was not rushing to say: “David
Cunliffe here to talk to you about my polic ies for the middle part of 2016.” It was like:
“Vote for us and you get the money.” Well, the Opposition has gone from yeah, nah to
yeah, nah, maybe. Read the fine print. They are Labour and the Greens. They would be
a high-spending and high-taxing Government if  they ever get there, which is good,
because that is the only high that Labour a nd the Greens look like they can agree on at
the moment.
Let us go to this Government and what it has actually achieved and what it is
actually delivering for New Zealanders. The programme today spells out where this
Government is going to go. But what is worthy of discussion is also where this
Government has been and whom the New Zealand public actually trust with New
Zealand. It is this Government, a National-le d Government, that has balanced the books
in this country and will see us back in surplus by 2014-15. It is this Government that
guided Christchurch through the tragedies of  the Christchurch earthquakes, stood
behind it, week after week after week, making sure it had the support that it needed. It
was this Government that guided the country  through the global financial crisis, to a
point where economic commentators around th e world talk about New Zealand as the
stand-out developed economy.
It is under this Government that 17,000 pe ople left a benefit last year and 1,500
people a week leave a benefit and get a job. It is under this Nati onal-led Government
that people are employed. It is under this Government that ACC rates are being reduced
for New Zealanders, for workers, for employ ees, across the board, and it is under this
National-led Government that when we look ou t there at the crime ra te in this country,
we see it is at a 33-year low.
It is this Government that can be trus ted to roll out ultra -fast broadband. I know
David Cunliffe is saying that he is goi ng to close down Facebook. That is actually
something that most leaders around the world ha ve not managed to do. But that is right.
That was today’s proclamation from David C unliffe—the fine print. He is going to
close down Facebook. That will be interesting. But this is also the Government with the
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15527
track record that has seen an enormous incr ease in elective surgical operations available
to New Zealanders. This is the Government  that stood up with a plan to prevent the
harm that is taking place in our communities against young children.
This Government and its plan is the reason that three-quarters of a billion dollars will
be spent this year in New Zealand on l ooking for oil and gas—because of this
Government. And actually, despite what Da vid Cunliffe said about his new-found
friends in Norway, it was Labour that had no rules in the exclusiv e economic zone, let
alone tough rules. It had no rules whatsoever , when it came to deep-sea drilling. Last
year, when we were in this House, Labour members were the ones being critical and all
of a sudden, miraculously, that has changed.
It is under this National-led Government th at housing will become more affordable,
because we have the right approach to fixing that issue. That is through the accords with
the Auckland Council and ultimately around the country. That is with making sure that
new land is released. That is with making sure that there are refinements to our
legislation, particularly over time, to th e Resource Management Act, to allow young
New Zealanders to buy a home.
It is this National-led Gove rnment that has stood up and is tackling the issues of
teacher performance and principal perfor mance, so that every young New Zealander
gets a chance to succeed, to do well, and to have a world-class education. That is what is
happening under this Governme nt. Under this Government Transmission Gully will be
built, like the Waterview Connection is.
In the plan for the year the Government goes back to the four key points that it has
been implementing for some time. To respons ibly manage finances—that has got to be
the top priority. I say to New Zealanders w ho see these other politic al parties offering
something that if it is too good to be true, it  probably is. When David Cunliffe tells you
he has found $1.5 billion at the end of a ra inbow and he is out spending it, roughly,
depending on whether you read the fine pr int, maybe, just maybe, you need to ask
where that is coming from. By the way, if you are earning $150,000 an d you are in that
category of poverty, according to Labour, you will also have your tax rate going up year
after year after year. And if you are a young couple who is buying the bakery in Hāwera
and you are trying to make a living, under Labour, it will put a capital gains tax on you,
because you are rich, and because you are out there trying to create employment,
because you care about trying to get other people a job. When Labour has done all that,
and when it has spent like it did last time it was in office—if it ever gets there again—
we know what happens. Interest rates go up. The competitive part of the economy goes
south, and a National-led Government has to come in and tidy things up.
Their heads are down over there for one reason and one  reason alone: they know it
does not add up. They know we are not even ou t the end of January and they have spent
three-quarters of a billion dollars with their mates the Gr eens—let alone everything that
happened last year. That is what New Zealan ders like about this plan and trust about
this Government—that in the course of 5 years we have  actually held Government
spending pretty much at the same rate, but we have prioritised what matters. At-risk
New Zealanders have had Working for Families maintained, pensions maintained, and
accommodation supplements maintained. This Government has reprioritised to ensure
that happens.
This Government will also stick to its pl an of building a competitive and productive
economy. It will continue to deliver bett er public services an d it will rebuild
Christchurch. Let us go through some indivi dual bits of the plan . Back in 2008, when
we became the Government, this is what Trea sury told us: the debt to GDP ratio was
going to 60 percent by 2020. Why? Because we were inheriting a bunch of the stuff we
saw yesterday: say anything, do anything to try to get there,  and try to tell people you
15528 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
are doing them a favour with their own money, until the music stops and you get booted
out, and someone actually has to come in a nd tidy the place up. What does this year’s
plan show? It shows that by 2014-15 we will not be a decade of deficits; we will be
back in surplus—we will back in surplus. Debt will have peaked at 26.5 percent, and by
2019-20 it will be at 17 percent—16.9 percen t. New Zealanders take enormous
confidence from that. This Government will work on repaying debt, because we actually
trust New Zealanders and they trust us to be able to take care of them when there is
actual need. When a Christchurch earthquake comes, a strong Government can stand in
support. A profligate one cannot.
When it come to competitiveness, this Government will remain committed to the
Business Growth Agenda and to expanding e xport markets. That includes trying to
complete our free-trade agreement with Korea,  with Russia, and with the Trans-Pacific
Partnership countries, not the least of th em being the United States. In 2014 this
Government will do something that parties on th e other side of the House talk about but
never actually support, and that is get behind the film industry. This is the Government
that saw over—Jacinda Ardern is shaking her head, but she was the Hobbit-hater, out
there saying not to create 5,500 jobs for the hobbits—5,500 jobs created. Now we have
got Avatar 2 , Avatar 3 , and Avatar 4  being made in New Zealand because of this
Government’s actions. That is what happens when you have good government.
We are committed to smart investment. We are committed to making sure that
science is at the heart of the Government. We will continue to work with Callaghan
Innovation in making sure that New Zeala nd firms and New Zealand businesses across
the country have the very best science av ailable to them. We will continue down the
path of our National Science Challenges and of our Primary Growth Partnership, and
making sure we use science to make New Zealand a more competitive economy.
When it comes to skills and in the workplace,  this Government will continue to do
that and it will ensure that we reach our target that 55 percent of 25 to 34-year-olds have
some sort of advanced trade qualification, diploma, or degree by 2017. There will be an
additional 4,500 places in trades and servic es academies, and this year alone over
10,000 people will have access to the Youth Guarantee—fees-free learning for 16 to 19-
year-olds under a National-led Government.
When it comes to safety in the workplace, that will be a priority for the Government
this year, as we look, through WorkSafe Ne w Zealand, to improve the culture in our
workplaces so that workers across New Zeal and can go to their place of work and be
confident that they will come home from their daily work. We will make sure that
WorkSafe New Zealand works with those industries that need support and need change
to ensure that that takes place.
We will make sure that ACC reductions continue to be delivered so that New
Zealanders can pay less for their ACC. When it comes to infrastructure, as I said earlier,
work on Transmission Gully will begin, wo rk will continue on the Christchurch
Western Corridor, work will continue on the Waikato Expre ssway, work will continue
on the Waterview Connection, not from borrowings—not from borrowings—but in
some part from proceeds of sales of minor assets in New Zealand companies that have
deepened our capital markets.
This party and this Government remain committed to ultra-fast broadband so that
every school in the country, ev ery hospital in the country, an d three-quarters of all New
Zealand homes can be wired to the world. We looked with great amazement and pride at
Lorde yesterday. She is a great example of  how New Zealand music was delivered over
the internet. Joel Little himself said that they produced that music to give away on the
internet and, in fact, it turned her into a singing sensation.
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15529
We will carry on our work around housing and addressing those issues, and
particularly Christchurch will remain an important part of the Government’s agenda, as
it has been since the Christchurch earthquak es. There are those anchor projects—the
justice precinct, over a billi on dollars going into schools and into housing. And when it
comes to education, we will not say that the answer to fixing the whole problem in the
education system is giving the odd kid a lu nch. That is not actu ally going to fix the
problem. What will fix the problem is paying $50,000 to a world-class principal to go in
and fix up a school that is failing those kids. Th at is what is going to fix their education.
We are going to say to those teachers to stay in the classroom, share your expertise, be
paid more for that, be an expert teacher, go around the other schools in your cluster, or
be an executive principal and expand that. We are going to continue with national
standards so that parents can understand the progress of their child, and we will
continue to work on moderation amongst schools.
We will continue our work in law and or der, because New Zealanders feel safer
under a National-led Government. We will con tinue with Addressing the Drivers of
Crime and rehabilitation. We will look to stre ngthen and expand the rights of victims in
legislation that makes it easier for children who are witnesses or for rape victims. We
will continue our work on cyber-bullying. As I said, when it comes to health, one of the
top priority areas for this Government is that we will continue to ensure that patients are
at the centre of what we focus on in our health system. We will make sure that they
continue to get access to elec tive surgery faster, we will c ontinue to make sure they
have world-class and gold-standard cancer tr eatment and that there is more money for
magnetic resonance imaging and CAT scans, a nd we will continue to make sure that
people can feel confident in what we are doing.
You can walk the walk or you can talk the talk. This is a National-led Government
that walks the walk. This is a National- led Government that has shown through the
work of the last 5 years, and will conti nue to show in 2014, that we are up for any
challenge that is put before us and that we can meet those ch allenges and deliver a
brighter future for New Zealanders. We are not going to sit there and try to bribe the
electorate with imaginary money that does not  exist. We are not going to ask people to
read the fine print, like a commercial cont ract, when I give a speech at a school
someplace in New Zealand. We are going to say to New Zealanders that they can trust
what we say, and they can trust us to de liver what we do. We are a good Government,
not a tricky Opposition. Bring on 2014.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: I move, That all the words
after “That” be deleted and replaced with “t his House express no confidence in this
National-led Government because New Zeal and has become more and more divided,
because those in the middle are struggling, and because the poor are going
backwards.” What is going to be that Prime Ministe r’s legacy when he finishes up later
this year? Just how is he going to be remembered? Well, it will not be for that
visionless, defensive speech full of tinkering and the same old, same old. It might be for
his half-finished, user-pays cycleway, but  I doubt it because “John Key Memorial
Cycleway” does not really have a certain ring to it. It might  be for the holiday home in
Hawaii. Hawaii, also known as “Planet Ke y”—the place where there are lots of golf
courses but no toilets, which will not be eas y for the President of the United States or
his security detail. Or it mi ght be for the Budget surpluse s that Labour always ran but
National has yet to sample. In  9 years of Labour Governme nt we never ran a fiscal
deficit and National has never run a surplus. Being lectured  on fiscal prudence by those
clowns is a bit like being lectured on tact and discernment by Gerry Brownlee.
I think that John Key is actually going to go down in  history by what the
international press calls him: “unidentified guest”. No wonder—the photo ops are about
15530 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
as flaky as his commitment to reducing une mployment. I think he is going to be
remembered for his true achievement: in s hort, fiddling while Rome burns—he is doing
it now—and for being the last gasp of an old, tired, failed way of doing things. He will
be remembered as the Prime Minister who cl ung to “business as usual” while every day
more and more Kiwis find themselves str uggling—left behind by a G overnment that is
increasingly out of touch, arrogant, and patently just in it for its mates. He talks about an
economic recovery, but let us be blunt. The only good news comes from the insurance
cheques from the disaster in Christchurch and some damn good prices for milk solids.
Neither of those can the Government take cr edit for. It does not milk the cows and it
does not milk the dairy markets.
Milk is New Zealand’s greatest export—ne arly a quarter of our export receipts.
When the price of milk powder goes up, our ec onomy goes up with it. That is all very
well if you have got a dairy farm, as half the National caucus seems to have—at least
one; sometimes five—but not much good if  you are trying to run a manufacturing
business and export something other than milk powder. It is not much good if you are
trying to do smart, value-added, sustaina ble business in a world where your future
seems dependent on the end of a cow’s udder.
If you take a devastated city and the price of milk out of the e quation, what are you
left with? An unidentified guest. But putting that aside and putting aside the fact that the
Government can claim no responsibility whatev er for any type of recovery, what is it
doing with what there is? I will tell you what it is doing. It is making sure that it goes to
the top few. That is the kind of recovery we are seeing—recovery in luxury car sales,
sales of million-dollar homes, profits of big corporations, and the record highs being
added on the rich list. It is in teresting to hear him talk about  it. He still puts his faith in
trickle-down theories, but 30 years of incr easing inequality, increasing child poverty,
and a shrinking middle New Zealand clearly says otherwise.
Unlike milking cows, this Government is  milking New Zeala nd, and it is called
“trickle up”, not trickle down, which would explain why the chequebook is always open
for big business but not for Pike River families. It is why it is happy for the employment
law to be changed for Warner Bros but there is not even a chance of an inquiry for the
families of dead forestry workers. It is why the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment would be happy to cough up a hundred grand for an Auckland to
Invercargill yacht race that never happened but  the Ministry of Social Development cut
a similar amount from a trust that helps disabl ed children. It is why there is a billion
dollars of tax cuts for the richest New Z ealanders but the most vulnerable get booted
when they cannot get a job. It explains why e lite private schools get tens of millions of
taxpayer funding, while a decile 1 Christchurch school gets unlawfully shut down.
It explains why major superm arkets are posting record profits and mums and dads
with good jobs struggle to keep up with the bi lls. It is why power companies are raking
in super-profits and retirees  are going without heating because they cannot afford to
open their power bills. It is why the stockb rokers who helped John Key sell our assets
made over $150 million on clipping the ticket while manufacturers that are trying to sell
real value-added Kiwi-made goods get a high do llar and lay-offs. It is why a select few
are making millions on investment prope rty tax-free and everybody else who works
hard, plays by the rules, and earns a salary or  a wage pays tax on every dollar they earn.
The top 1 percent under John Key owns 16 perc ent of the wealth, and the bottom half
owns only one-twentieth.
Like I said, the Government is arrogant, ou t of touch, and out for its mates. I am
struck by just how out of touch it is when I hear Mr Key talking about safe and skilled
workplaces—tell that to the families of th e dead forestry workers or the miners—and
about a so-called commitment to export markets,  which is code for trade deals he will
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15531
not even let the public see. There is one commitment that New Zealand would like to
see, and that is a commitment to loweri ng our dollar right now, because the Reserve
Bank says that we are 15 percent overvalued, a nd that adds up to jobs lost and families
ruined. And that is not even scratching the su rface. Listen to the Prime Minister and his
southern henchman Mr English and Mr Joyce and they will tell you that you should
count yourself lucky, that this is as good as it ge ts, and that there is no alternative. I will
tell you something. There is an alternativ e, and that is called a new Labour-led
Government.
Just yesterday in my state of the nation speech I outlined the vision for a better New
Zealand, a fairer New Zeala nd, one where everybody has the opportunity to make the
most of themselves—the kinds of opportunitie s that both the Prim e Minister and I had
when we were young. Neither of us came from  families that had any money. We both
benefited from a good State school. We benef ited from a good health system when my
dad was desperately ill. But John Key has been pulling the ladder up after himself. He is
continuing his 30-year project of widening the gap between the haves and have-nots,
and that is not a future that we want for Ne w Zealand. It is not one that New Zealanders
want for themselves.
We are a fair nation and we value attri butes like hard work and compassion and
looking after each other, because we know that when some of us do well, we all should
do well. It should not be to pit New Zealander against New Zealander. It should not be
to pit the 1 percent against the 99 percent. I think that, actually, in his heart of hearts,
that is something that even the Prime Minist er recognised when he launched his little
pet teacher bonus scheme last week. It was a pretty clumsy shot at softening his image.
He even used the word “egalitarian” and—w ait for it—a rugby analogy, and I just think
that I am soon going to see a pi cture of him as an unidentifie d guest at a barbecue with
Prince William. Predictable.
Never before, though, in all seriousness, ha s New Zealand faced the critical choices
it faces now. We are at a crossroads. One pa th points to an increasingly fractured and
divided society, a widening gap between the haves and the have-nots, a Government
that is arrogant, out of t ouch, and out for its mates. We  want a better, fairer New
Zealand. The other path is one  of courage, of compassion, and of ingenuity. We want a
country that embodies all that is good about our past and combines it with our highest
vision for a modern, fair, inclusive economy. It means building an economy worthy of
our Kiwi values, a country based on those values—and with good clean water; the water
in my glass just now was very good.
In that New Zealand a full day’s work will cover the basics. There will be more jobs
available, and wages will catch up with prices. New Zealanders will pay what is fair
whether it is for their power bill, their tax b ill, or their grocery bill. Every child in the
country will have what they deserve: a fair  chance, an opportunity to make the best of
themselves, to work hard and to get ahead, to start life healthy, to  learn early, and to
fulfil their potential.
It is not just the right thing to do, it is the smart thing to do, because when every Kiwi
kid can be the best they can be, this country will be the best it can be. It will be a
successful economy with strong regions, with  investment, with training, and with
research and development, not just a speculato r’s paradise or some foreigner’s farm. It
will be an economy with strong regions wher e there are good jobs for all who need
them, a networked, digital economy with fa ster, cheaper broadband rolled out faster
than those clowns could roll out a roll of toilet paper. It will be an economy with decent
work, good conditions, high wage s, and safe workplaces, an economy built on a world-
leading education system with high-value exports.
15532 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
New Zealand is not going to get rich by e xporting raw logs or raw milk powder or
bulk fish caught on foreign vessels by fore ign crews who are no t paid the minimum
wage, who do not pay tax in New Zealand, an d who export the processing offshore; or
by a freezing industry riddled with overcapac ity that is now exporting whole carcasses
so somebody else can cut them up and add the value; or by limiting a technology
industry with inadequate, overpriced broadband—[Interruption] I say to Ms Adams—or
by cutting research and development funding for our most innovative industries.
Over the next few months the Labour Part y will be launching a series of joined-up
policy packages designed to rebuild and re balance this economy, from this country,
from local communities up, and with it we will outline how the economy needs to work
for New Zealanders both now and in the fu ture. We started yesterday with our Best
Start package, a set of policie s that is about giving the ne xt generation the best start
possible: 59,000 families with newborn babies will receive a Best St art payment of $60
a week for the first year of the child’s life. The investment will go to all families with a
combined income of $150,000 or less in their first year, and it will give them more
choices about how they juggle work and home life. We need to keep easing the pressure
for modest and middle-income families beyond  the first year. That is why for those
families earning up to $50,000, the payment of $60 will continue unabated to the child’s
third birthday.
I also announced that we will be increasing free early childhood education to 25
hours, up from 20 hours. We all know that  early childhood education makes a real
difference, and the experts tell us that the return is $11 for every $1 invested. Alongside
that we need to expand access to early childhood centres, because free hours are not
enough if you have not got a centre to study in, and we need to restore funding for
qualified teachers.
Why is it that that Prime Minister will pa y bonuses to high school principals and cut
funding for early childhood educat ors? Come to think of it, why is it that Hekia Parata
cuts teacher development for all teachers so that the National Government can pay
bonuses to a few top teachers? Does it want el ites in our schools as well as everywhere
else? Oh, I forgot. You are allowed more s ubsidies if you are a pr ivate school, or a
charter school, where you do not have to teach the New Zealand curriculum, you do not
even have to have a qualified teacher, and you are not subjec t to the Official
Information Act. For that special treatment, you get paid extra by the National
Government.
By contrast, in partnership with commun ities, Labour will fund the development of
early childhood education centr es in lower-income communiti es to ensure there are
places for every Kiwi kid, and we are committed to funding 26 weeks of paid parental
leave for every New Zealand family that needs it. This is interesting. What are members
opposite going to do? They told us that they  were committed to working this through.
Now they say that they are going to veto our bi ll just so that they can bring in a smaller
one of their own. That is like John Key sa ying to Barack Obam a: “No, you can have
your driver back. I’m going to drive with the pu tter.” It is the sort of lack of integrity
that people are coming to expect from a Government that is not looking after New
Zealanders but is just looking after its mates.
Success in the early years invo lves health as well as educ ation. That is why we are
going to make sure pregnant mums get booked in for antenatal checks at 10 weeks. That
is why every expectant mum will be able to get free childcare training classes when they
are pregnant, that is why we will extent well child checks, and that is why we will
provide early access to early childhood educat ion for those families who need it. The
Best Start package will ensure parents have more choices and better support so that their
kids get better opportunities and New Zealand gets a better future.
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15533
I am reminded of Mr Key’s comments a few years ago, when he described women
on the DPB as “breeding for a business”. How telling about Mr Key’ s values. This is a
morally bankrupt Government. It is old, it is  tired, and it is, as we can see from the
number of Nats getting off the sinki ng ship, on its way out —on its way out. The
challenge before New Zealanders in this decisive election year is to restore values,
restore heart, restore opportunity, and restore equality.
The Labour-led Government is waiting to take New Zealand forward. We are waiting
for this Government to hasten out of office so that this country can get a new tomorrow,
a best start for our kids, a best start for New Zealand. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: The 2014 election offers New
Zealanders the opportunity to make history by electing the first ge nuinely progressive
Government in more than a generation. Th e 2014 election offers New Zealanders the
opportunity to make history by voting for a strong Green Party at the heart of a
progressive Government. There are few elections that can genuinely claim to be turning
points in history, few elections that can genui nely claim to be forks in the road of
history, but the 2014 election will be such an election. The result of this election will be
either a forward-looking, progressive Gove rnment—a reforming Government in the
tradition of Seddon, Savage, and Kirk—or a right-wing, throwback Government, the
likes of which we have not seen since Ruth Richardson.
In the last 24 hours the contrasting values of these two a lternatives have been very
clear. The Green Party has proposed spendi ng $100 million a year to ensure that poor
kids at school have food in their stomachs and access to health care. The National Party
has attacked this policy, ye t this is the same National Party that is spending $1,000
million a year on tax cuts for the top 10 percent of income earners. Green Party values
lead us to prioritise spending $100 million a year giving food and health care to hungry,
sick New Zealand schoolchildren. National Party values lead it to prioritise spending 10
times that amount—$1 billion a year—giving more money to the top 10 percent of
income earners. The choice of values is stark. Is it any wonder that the Prime Minister’s
statement did not mention children? In 2014 New Zealanders will get to choose which
kinds of values they want in their Government.
New Zealand has a strong history of wo rld-leading, progressive, reforming
Governments. The Liberal Government of the 1890s introduced the old-age pension and
women’s suffrage. The Liberals worked with  unions to protect working people while
developing the New Zealand economy. They started our public health system. Forty
years after the great reforms of the Liberals, in the 1930s, the Savage Government led
the world in introducing a social welfare Stat e that treated people with humanity in the
midst of the Great Depression. The social and economic policies introduced by the
Savage Government led the world, and afte r the Second World War they were adopted
and admired across the world. The New Z ealand economy boomed under the settings
established by Savage. Forty years after th e reforms of the Savage Government, the
1970s Kirk Government updated the welfare State by introducing such things as a
domestic purposes benefit for single mums. It  staked out an independent South Pacific
foreign policy by protesting against French nuclear testing. It stood up to apartheid by
blocking the tour of an apartheid rugby team, because, unlike our current Prime
Minister, “Big Norm” knew whether he was fo r or against apartheid. It established the
Waitangi Tribunal and returned the minimum wage to 66 percent of the average wage.
These three progressive reforming G overnments—Seddon, Savage, and Kirk—were
far from perfect, and some of Seddon’s view s on race were offensive, but they changed
the course of history and they made life better for ordinary New Zealanders. They set up
New Zealand as a world leader. Forty years after the Kirk Government, it is time again
for a new wave of progressive Government re form in New Zealand. It is time to refresh
15534 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
the progressive vision for Aot earoa New Zealand. It is time for a Green Government. It
is time for a Green Government that reinvigorates our co mmon, progressive
commitment to the values of egalitarianis m, sovereignty, and democracy. More than
that, we need a Green Government that integrates these historically important
progressive values with the new, modern values of sustainability. We need a Green
Government committed to fairness, independence, democracy, and sustainability.
The next wave of progressive change that  is sweeping the world is green. The green
revolution is transforming the way we live on planet Earth as we learn to live good lives
on a finite planet with limited natural res ources. We are learning to access the unlimited
resources of human creativity, ingenuity, and generosity in order to live prosperous
lives within limited natural resources. That  is why smart and green go together. We
need to learn how to live smarter so that we can have prosperity while recognising the
natural limits of a finite planet. Unleashing human innovation, creativity, and generosity
so that we can all live good lives while lo ving and protecting our natural environment is
what the green movement is all about.
History is, of course, littere d with those who said that progressive change was not
possible, those who opposed women’s suffrage , racial equality, the welfare State,
homosexual law reform, public health, and public education. They opposed nuclear-free
New Zealand and cannot remember whether they  are for or against apartheid. They said
that clean energy was impossible. How wrong they were. Renewable electricity
generation is now the fastest-growing sector of electricity generation in the world, set to
overtake gas generation as the second-largest source of electricity in the world in the
next couple of years, accord ing to the International Energy Agency. Green jobs are the
fastest-growing sector of the economy. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics found that
the greener the industry, the higher the rate  of job growth over the last decade. The
clean energy future is here, and those w ho railed against it are now seeing our new
reality happening before their very eyes. S o, yes, there are those who will rail against
history and against the green movement, but th ey have always been there, and yet we
have made history before and we will make it again.
But as I said at the start of  this speech, this election is  a turning point. Although on
the one hand we have the choice of a genuinely progressive Government, the alternative
if the current Government is given a third term will be a very different Government
from that elected in 2008. It will be a hard right Government, economically,
environmentally, and socially, beholden to  the damaged and di scredited ACT Party,
United Future party, and Conservative Party.
John Key’s claim to be a moderate has evapor ated over the last couple of years. He
has overseen increasing water pollution, blocked attempts to set strong rules to clean up
our rivers, and subsidised polluting irrigation schemes. The Government has destroyed a
price on carbon and subsidised fossil fuel s, with the result that New Zealand’s
greenhouse emissions are projected to incr ease 50 percent above 1990 levels by 2030
according to the Ministry for the Environment’s own projections.
This Government has made it much harder for people just to get by. There are 50,000
more people unemployed than when John Key first came to power. Median household
income has fallen 4 percent after inflation under this National Government. Electricity
prices were up 3 percen t last year, despite falling dema nd. Rising mortgage rates this
year will wipe out any pay increases many fa milies get. This Government has failed to
manage the economy. Its irresponsible tax cu ts to the to p 10 percent, costing $1.1
billion a year, have contributed to National’ s record borrowing. In just 6 years National
has borrowed more than all prior Governments combined. National’s economic priority,
asset sales, has failed and has cost taxpayers $440 million so far.
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15535
But this will be nothing compared with what  will happen if the National Party is re-
elected. The first thing, I bet, is that John Key will not stay a full term as Prime
Minister. He will be replaced by someone even further to the right, like Steven Joyce or
Judith Collins. The second thing is that Nati onal can be re-elected  only if it has the
support of the Conservative Party, a party that wants to roll back all of the gains made
in the last 30 years for the rights of wo men, gay and lesbian New Zealanders, and
children. Such a hard right Government will further turn its back on science—climate
science in particular, as Tony Abbott is doing across the Ditch. Such a hard right
Government will take away the ladder of opport unity that many of us here climbed to
achieve our potential. It will embrace the politics of the conservative right, which
believes that a woman’s place is in the kitche n and a gay man’s place is in the closet,
and it will turn its back on New Zealand’s opp ortunity to be a world leader in green
economics and green jobs. That is what we will get if we have a third term of a National

items.speaker: Government. The choice is stark
items.text: a br oad, inclusive, progressive, reforming
Government or a narrow, ideological Government of the far right.
Alongside the historic gains in economic, social, and environment policy that have
been achieved over the years by progressive activists and Governments, there is one
other important achievement that is wort h celebrating this year , and that is the
proportional voting system, MMP. The year 2014 is the 18 th anniversary of MMP.
MMP has come of age. The new generation of  voters who will get to vote for the first
time this year has known New Zealand onl y under MMP. These young voters did not
have to experience what it was like to vote  in a first-past-the- post election, with the
winner-takes-all system that left the major ity of voters without representation in the
Government. First past the post produced Governments that had the support of a
minority of voters but that had almost absolute power. It probably seems inconceivable
to those young voters that we had elections wh ere a party could have a majority of MPs
and form a Government with only 35 percen t of the vote, as was the case with the
National Government elected in 1993.
Under MMP a party share of th e popular vote is directly proportional to its share of
seats in Parliament. Those who campaigned for MMP, like Rod Donald, were working
to deepen and strengthen our democracy, but under this Government democracy is
being hollowed out. Under this Government Ne w Zealand has been denied the best of
MMP. In fact, John Key is now telling us that  he should automatically get to form the
next Government and be Prime Minister even if he has the support of only a minority of
voters. It is worth repeating this, because it is quite outrageous: the Prime Minister is
saying that he should get to lead the next Government even if he has the support of only
a minority of voters. That is his take on democracy. I do not think that he really
understands why New Zealanders voted for MMP.
MMP was about bringing an end to the era where one perso n, like Robert Muldoon
or Roger Douglas or Ruth Richardson, c ould force through their unpopular agenda. But
John Key and Steven Joyce have  returned us to that worl d MMP was meant to be about
Governments respecting the opinions of ot hers. Coalition Governments, cross-party
select committees—these were supposed to mean something, to be a check on executive
power rather than the rubber stamp they have become.
But this Government has used its power to ignore the will of the people. It showed its
arrogance and blatantly flouted democracy by  publicly stating before voting had even
begun that it would ignore the results of the citizens initiated referendum on asset sales.
We saw exactly the same behaviour when this Government decided to ignore the results
of the MMP review for purely partisan, political reasons. New Zealanders voted to keep
MMP at the 2011 referendum, and then thousan ds of New Zealanders took part in the
review to make MMP even fairer. The Gove rnment was given a very clear steer by the
15536 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
public and the independent umpire, the El ectoral Commission, on what changes the
public wanted—in particular, abolishing the coat-tailing provision, which has allowed
this National Government to do its dirty deals and cobble together a Government.
Acting in pure self-interest,  National ignored the will of the people and left MMP
unchanged. It undermined our electoral syst em, and now John Key is doing dirty coat-
tailing deals all over the country just to keep his political options alive in this election.
MMP is not supposed to be about one part y struggling to maintain power by relying
on a couple of dodgy hangers-on. MMP is  not about the bigge st minority party
automatically having the right to govern. It is about forming Governments with majority
support. But this Government, with its single-vote majority and its unstable and
unethical coalition reliant on disgraced MPs, has forced things through against the will
of the majority of New Zealanders. Entirel y because of the support of Peter Dunne and
John Banks, this Government has been allowed to pass into law a series of obscene
policies.
Firstly, it sold off the assets built up ove r generations, transferring the wealth from
the 99 percent to the 1 percent. It attacked  our privacy, our freedom, and our liberty. It
passed the Search and Surveillance Bill, the Government Communications Security
Bureau Amendment Bill, and the Telecommun ications (Interception Capability and
Security) Bill. The role  of the State is supposed to be to protect human rights and civil
liberties, but instead the National Party has passed laws that rest rict our freedom of
expression and our freedom to live free from  State surveillance. It attacked local
democracy as well as removing the vote from Cantabrians even before the earthquake. It
also showed that it does not  understand, respect, or trus t local government or local
communities by undermining the independence of local government.
The National Government attacks the most vulnerable people in our society: the sick,
the young, vulnerable women, and the disabled and those caring for them. It introduced
unacceptable discrimination into our law through youth rates, telling young people they
are not worthy of our respect, and reinfor ced New Zealand as a low-wage economy.
With the support of the M āori Party it removed the rights of  family carers of disabled
people to have their day in court. It rushed that law change through this Parliament in a
single day. Muldoon would be proud.
The National Government attacks the envi ronment. It weakened the emissions
trading scheme, facilitate d the exploitation of sche dule 4 conservation land, and
polluted our rivers. It threaten ed to lock up the defenders of the environment if they
went anywhere near an oil rig or an oil ve ssel. It facilitated a morally contemptible,
dirty, dodgy deal, swapping gambling laws for a convention centre. All of these
disgraceful changes to our laws were pos sible only because of the support of Peter
Dunne, whom the Prime Minister tells us he  does not trust, and John Banks, who is in
front of the courts for elector al fraud. This is how this Government has undermined the
promise of MMP and our democracy.
But New Zealanders can take back the power  this year. New Zealanders have a real
chance to elect a truly modern MMP coali tion. True MMP is about stable government
where the majority of New Zealanders are re presented in a strong coalition of strong
partners. It is about principled parties coming together and working towards policies
that meet the needs of New Zealanders. It is  about a Government that is representative
and has a range of smart new voi ces at the table. This is what MMP should be. This is
what those who fought for MMP were fighting for.
As MMP turns 18 it is time for New Zeal and to have a true MMP Government—
MMP as it should be. It is ti me for a strong, progressive Government. It is time for a
Green Government. The Green Party is ready to  govern. We are ready to sit at the table
and deliver real gains for real people. Yes, we will compromise—MMP requires that of
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15537
all partners in a coalition—but we will not co mpromise on our principles or our values.
We have the ideas, the experience, and the credentials. We have been a parliamentary
voice for change since 1999, and we are more than ready to make a real green change in
Government. We have stable leadership s upported by our team of MPs who are smart,
progressive, forward thinkers. We have an experienced party orga nisation and a strong
grassroots membership. We have made real  changes already in New Zealanders’ lives.
We have warmer homes, cleaner food, and be tter transport options as a result of our
work. We set the agenda and we follow th rough with solutions. In Government we will
achieve even more. A strong Green Party in Government will focus on building a
sustainable economy, dismantling inequality, an d protecting our environment. We will
build on our wins to make sure that we have a smarter, cleaner, more compassionate
country for all New Zealanders. Bring on the election.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The Prime Minister wants the
House to express its confidence in the Nati onal Government. Well, we do not. The plan
outlined by the Prime Minister for 2014 brought to mind the word “hoover”—not the
great water dam in the United States, and not the first FBI boss in the United States, but
the vacuum cleaner. You know why? Becaus e it sucks. John Key has spent too long
running around after the movie moguls. He is in his own fantasy land. His speech had
the most confused start of a ny speech that I have ever heard by a party leader in this
House—the most confused start that I have ever heard.
And then the anxiety when he looked to Gerry for help! His speech should have been
an honest and objective statement of the c onditions facing the count ry, the challenges
ahead, and the solutions the Government has to  offer, which are all the big things that
matter to ordinary people. Instead, it was pu re spin and manipulation and deceit, and
incorrect statements. New Zealand Prime Mi nisters of the past would have been
embarrassed to have spouted such dribble. I th ink that a leadership spill in the National
Party is not long away. Gerry is smiling, because  he may be able to get on the right side
and perhaps prolong his alrea dy far too long career. But I k now that it is going on. My
inside information tells me that.
National is a Government of non-achievers with a woeful record of failure. It always
puts the interests of foreign big business ahead of ordinary  New Zealanders. It keeps
selling valuable State assets in a process that can only be characterised as economic
madness. Here are some of the many exampl es of economic failure. There are 150,000
New Zealanders unemployed, while immigrant work visas and permanent residencies—

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Come on—anti-immigration.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: —are sold like expensive bus tickets. That member
saw Campbell Live last night. He should watch it ag ain tonight. All over the country it
is going on, and the member from Hamilton Ea st, Mr Bennett, thinks it is a laughing
matter. It is not. It is an abomination to a First World c ountry and to First World laws.
There is a housing crisis, but the Governme nt refuses to acknowledge that migrant
numbers and overseas speculators are creatin g havoc and are cheat ing Kiwis out of a
decent home. There is not one country in As ia that would tolera te such a policy. The
Government could not find one politician in  Asia who would support such a policy, so
why is it doing it to its own people?
Nothing has been done to address the massive overseas debt. Here is what is worse—
the Prime Minister did not admit it, but it is all in the documentation—the massive
overseas debt is not coming down; it is going up. That is why he uses 2020 figures and
2021 figures. Look, he will be gone a long time before that. In fact, there will not be one
member there left—possibly we will be, for obvious reasons. But th ere will not be one
member there left, and those members are using figures that they first started to use in
2008—12 years away from 2020—and now they ar e still talking about 2020 like they
15538 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
are going to hold on until then. I do not think so. It is still rising. The exchange rate is
crippling exporters and manufact urers, and again the Government refuses to act. It is
paralysed. Worse still, it contemplates an offici al cash rate rise shortly, which will boot
up mortgage rates, and then what will happen as well is that it will kick up the exchange
rate even further.

items.speaker: Here it is today
items.text: Mr English, trying to show  that he is in control. He says he is
concerned about the high exchange rate, and that it was a con cern for the economy.
Whoop-de-do! We have got a finance Minister—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: The penny’s dropped!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The penny has finally dropped. He has been here for
far too long. He has been the finance Minist er for far too long. You have got people
saying that our currency will possibly reach pa rity with Australia. It is doing enormous
damage to an export-dependent nation, and what  does he say? “Well, so, it’s a bit of a
concern.” Oh, and this is what he also said, though. He said this, which absolutely belies
what the Prime Minister was saying: “I think it’s too high, ye s, and I think the
Australian economy is a bit stronger relative to ours.”—relative to ours.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: That’s a concession.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: That is a concession. He says that that indicates that,
all in the one quote. In the House, and out in front of the National Party’s cannon
fodder, he persuades them by saying one thing, but privately he has to admit that things
are seriously going wrong with the high currency.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Amazing what a week in Davos does.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Yeah, well, that is what a week in Davos does. Mind
you, half of that backbench over there do not know where Davos is.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: They thought it was on the West Coast!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Those members think it is on the West Coast,
between Hokitika and Greymouth. Worse still, as I say, they contemplate the official
cash rate going up, and up will go the dollar even further. And then they will say:
“Well, that’s a sign of a he althy economy.” It is unbelie vable the kind of economic
drivel that they get people like Mr Hayes and Mr Bennett to keep on repeating. I know
those two gentlemen, and privately they are alarmed. They know in their hearts that that
threatens their election prospects. I know Mr Hayes is smart. He is jumping ship now.
He is getting out now. He is getting pushed, and he is jumping now because he is wise.
He does not want to be sta nding around amidst the mayhem and debris of chaos, post
election night 2014, whenever National flies the white flag. Mr Hayes is an experienced
man. He knows he can smell danger. Mr Be nnett should pay attention, as Mr Hayes can
help you.
Let us look specifically at the economy. No effort will be spared by the National
Party to pump up the feel-good factor in advance of the 2014 el ection. “Mr Spray and
Walk Away” thinks he can pull it off one mo re time, but I have got bad news for him.
He cannot—he cannot. All the storm clouds are assembling now. Within the National
Party ranks, they look ready now for an alternative leader.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh yes, they are. Just because Hekia Parata is not
part of the cabal does not mean it is not going on. In fact, I think Hekia will be the first
tragedy when it takes place. There will be lots of talk of an economy firing on all
cylinders, the rock-star economy, which sti ll cannot match New Caledonia, by the way,
going at 3.5 year after year. National has had stagnated, bottlenecked, corked-up
growth, it gets it for a temporary, 1-year te rm, and it starts talking about the rock-star
economy. What a joke. No effort will be made to dispel or challenge the spin that New
Zealand is a rock-star—a superstar—economy. Well, look at all the fundamentals. It
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15539
ain’t true. A responsible Government would have immediately corrected this sort of
false and misleading claptrap.
Let me sound a warning about th is rock-star economy. It is only a suggestion, Gerry,
but do not forget who is making it. Treas ury has never won a Grammy award for
accuracy of its forecasts. It has never won—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who wrote that, Winnie?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, actually, Treasury wr ote it. Thanks for asking
the question. I could not have done better myself for timing. It is here and it says this—
this is from November last, the 5 months  ended 30 November: “T he operating balance
before gains and losses (OBEGAL) was in  deficit by $2.3 billi on, which was around
$400 million more than expected, mainly due to lower core Crown tax revenue.” Who
wrote that? Why, it is from the Government itself! It is from the Financial Statements of
the Government of New Zealand for the 5 months ended 30 November 2013. You see,
an $86 million surplus is cigarette-paper thin, and you are getting there because the
Government is suspending spending, like, for example, on overseas aid, whereas the
others spent $92 million last year, and like,  for example, suspending certain roading
projects. Just hold them back. Those member s think: “We will get a surplus any which
way we can, like we will hold back some Waita ngi settlements. We will not pay out to
these victims of the Viet Nam War. We just wi ll not do anything like that there, and we
think we will con our way through it.” I have to tell those members that it has all been
tried before and it always fails. Do not let it happen again.
As I said, only a few days ago Treasury forecast that this so-called deficit was not
going to be what it thought it would be. National, aided and abetted by its pet
intellectuals—and, yes, its puppets, bank economists, money traders, and corporate
cheerleaders—will put a positive spin on every bit of economic news, even when it is
bad. The facts are staring us in the face. Our manufacturers and exporters will get no
help, with an overvalued dollar. Bill Eng lish said today about the Aussie dollar itself
that it is going up by the day. It will keep going up, as I said, if interest rates are
increased. But National could not care less about every manufacturer, whether they have
closed or moved offshore. In the halcyon da ys of our great count ry, when National was
a good party and knew what it was doing, and had practical men of experience, we used
to rock on at 4.5 percent per year and manufacturing was 33 percent of our economy—
the GDP. Now it is 13 percent and falling, a nd the Government has no plan, because
manufacturing means offshore exports and it means jobs. It does not have a plan. Its
plan is hands-off and to let the free market work it out.
I know the apologist from Epso m thinks that that is a gr eat policy. He also thinks
that pulling down your hoardings when you are campaigning—not on election eve,
which the law requires. No, he pulls them down during the actual campaign itself.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: You couldn’t win an electorate.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, really? Let me tell that  member that I have won
electorates that no one else could win. We won all the M āori seats once. Nobody else
would be able to do that. We won all of them.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: What happened then?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: What happened was they got duped by their National
Party colleagues and failed to show the loya lty, and that is why the National Party is
now in trouble. It is because the Māori Party that they put—

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Andrew Williams wants to go.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: No, no. Mr Key made a speech last week, if you
recall, and all of sudden he says: “Oh, we w ill be happy to talk to New Zealand First.”
You know, it is a bit like that famous quote from Jesse Jackson, when he said that it
15540 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
seems like that when Santa Claus is running in to heavy weather, he decides that now he
will call upon Rudolph. It is unbelievable—unbelievable.
There is no basis for this National Governme nt to boast about its economic record.
Export prices for dairy produce have been at  record levels. New Zealand has been the
beneficiary of the best terms of trade for 40 years. There is nothi ng great or glorious
about 150,000 New Zealanders not being able to get a job. Wh at is so brilliant about
creating a speculative housing bubb le for foreign speculators in  Auckland? Is this part
of some brilliant economic plan known only to  the inner circle, or what they have
politely termed the “kitchen cabinet”? Do you see that phrase the “kitchen cabinet”?
Well, I know some of them have spent too mu ch time in the kitche n, but they do not
make a good—
Denis O’Rourke: Or in the dining room.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Or they are the product of  the kitchen, but they are
not a kitchen cabinet. As I said, New Zealand’ s external balance sheet is in an awful
state. The dollar is going up, and over the past 5 years National has failed totally to
diversify our economic base. We are now even  more vulnerable to what is known as a
black swan, or an unforeseen event or shock. That is wh ere we sit today, and wise
people have said it.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: What about the film industry?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Nick Smith asks what I will do about it. Well, let me
tell you. We have an economy based on, or  characterised by, one dominant export
product, which is milk powder; one dominan t export company, which is Fonterra; one
dominant export market, which is China; and one dominant import, which is people—
immigration. That is not a plan that a pa rty calling itself National, which would evince
putting its people first, should ever be proud of.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Anti-migrants—anti-migration.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The stark, ugly truth is th at New Zealand is nowhere
near paying its way in the world, Mr Bennett. It is clear that this Government is clueless
as to how to address that.
Young New Zealanders have been betrayed  by this Government. Their hopes of
homeownership have been snatched away. Barely any young coupl e can save at the
speed of soaring house price inflation, and, Mr Bennett, you cannot save that fast,
either. No member over there can save that fast—oh, maybe Mr Key can. But, of
course, that is Merrill Lynch. The rest cannot . None of those members can save that
fast, to match housing inflation. Young New Z ealanders struggle und er the burden of
