student debt, and their prospects of a dece nt, secure, and well-pa ying job have been
trashed by wholesale immigration policies.
Immigration is the most thriving and corrupt industry in New Zealand today. It is not
a laughing matter. It is all laid out there,  and you will hear a lot more as these few
months unfold in the term to come. Incredibly, over 150,000 migrant work visas were
issued in the year to June 2013—150,000. Toda y the Prime Minister announced more
work visas, and the whole process, he said, of issuing visas is go ing to be sped up.
Apply online—get a visa online. Come to New Zealand and take a Kiwi’s job! This is
lunacy and it is going to be stopped.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Are you going to stop it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Most certainly it is going to be stopped.
Just a point on what the Prime Minister clai med in the House this afternoon. He said
that the Hobbit movies created 5,500 jobs. That is wh at he said. They know over there
that that statement is bulldust.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No, it’s not.
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15541

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh no? Well, this is direct from the Prime Minister’s
office—his senior adviser. It  says this: “The PM was as king yesterday for the total
number of people who will work on both Hobbit movies. The context, if he is asked
about Labour’s industrial relations policy and how it might impact on the New Zealand
film industry, is he can say something like ‘About 3,000 people will work on the Hobbit
movies.’ If that policy had been in place, th en all those people might never have got a
job.” So it is 3,000 by gu ess here; now it is 5,500 . But he is not going to get away with
that sort of stuff in this campaign—oh no, sirree. We will be waiting there every time he
tells a porky—wahoo, exposure. He goes on to say this: “Would it be possible to get an
estimated number—just to the nearest 500 or 1,000 would be fine.” That is straight from
the senior adviser of the Prime Minister, a nd the Prime Minister gets up in the House
and tells people something else. He is misleading the House again.
The Government has no idea of who or what is coming into the country. Why should
New Zealanders give up their jobs to immigrants? The Gove rnment is not loyal to the
people of this country. Sure , it is a Government for the people. Sure, National is a
Government for the people—the people of Ch ina, India, anywhere but New Zealand.
The winter is going to be tough. Jobs will be  hard to get and power bills are going
through the roof. As for the statement about  increasing competition in the electricity
industry—well, that was pure garbage. We a ll know we have got a price-fixing cartel
operating here. Domestic consumers pay up to three times more for their power than big
companies do, and many small businesses and domestic consumers are being ripped off.
We all know it. It is an exer cise in deception, as is the broadband roll-out. A Southern
Cross cable conglomerate of Telecom and Chorus is exploiting New Zealand, the
Government, and the taxpayers , because the Government is  paying them more than
twice what it is worth—over $1 billion. So mehow the Government is trying to put
across that it is doing consumers a favour, when they have actually been ripped off.
It is just like the plan for the police. It is all about glib words. Do you know what the
Government said today? It said that the Government is going to reduce the rate of crime
by 15 percent—the rate of violent crime by 15 percent and the rate of youth crime by 25
percent. What a brazen abuse of figures a nd statistics. It sounds  something like the
police files out of North Korea and P yongyang. It does not sound like a First World
country. Has the Government told offenders  how much to reduce their offending? Who
is negotiating with the criminal community over these statistics? It is  an absolute fact
that if you do not have sufficient law enfor cement resources, then you will not have the
capacity to fight crime and much crime will go unreported. We know that on that
matter, New Zealand First is the only party with a great record. Last time we had the
power, we got 1,000 extra frontline police, ju st like that. Now the Government runs
around the place talking about the police resources.
The Government is even claiming that they brought in free medicine for under-6-
year-olds.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: No, Mr Key is claiming that boldly out on the public
stage. Thank heavens people remember. [ Bell rung] Two minutes to go, Mr Speaker?
One minute to go? Wonderful. That will be enough to finish off this party.
What we have heard today, if you look at the penultimate page, is  a statement about
taking steps this year to introduce a National match-fixing policy. That is what we heard
today—National’s match-fixing policy for the election. If you ca nnot win the game,
cheat or fix it. Well, we are on red alert and ready to hand out a card. We cannot say it
will be a red card. We cannot say it will be a green card. We cannot  say it will be a
yellow card. But we most definitely can say th at it will be a white  card. It will be a
white and black card as soon as National—as it will—flies the white flag.
15542 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014

items.speaker: One last statement
items.text: remember what Mr Key said about the SIS raid last year? He said
he did not know about it. We will prove in this House that he did.

items.speaker: Hon TARIANA TURIA
items.text: Mr Speaker, may I formally
acknowledge you and all other members at the onset of this important year, a year in
which I hope we can genuinely work together for the best interests of all who call this
land home. For many political commentato rs, the year begins with the annual
pilgrimage to R ātana P ā. I acknowledge, therefore, th e enduring legacy of Tahup ōtiki
Wīremu Rātana, the significance of his teachings encompassed in the Ture Wairua, and
the ongoing relevance of his message for Tu re Tangata. The message of Ture Tangata,
of course, deals with te mana  motuhake, the concerns of tangata w’enua for our land
claims, and our rights and res ponsibilities as embodied  in Te Tiriti o Waitangi. It is a
very strong basis for establishing our prioriti es for the year, and it is always pleasing
when those coming to the pā acknowledge those dual objectives of our nationhood.
This year, however, Winston Peters chose the moment to attack the M āori Party for
what he labelled apartheid policies. I cannot  let such an outrageous claim stand, and I
have deliberately waited for this first spe ech in the House this year to remind all
politicians of our moral and ethical responsib ility in the use we make of language for
effect. For the record, the crime of aparthei d, as stated by the 2002 Rome Statute of the
International Criminal Court, is defined as  inhumane acts of crimes against humanity
“committed in the context of an institutiona lized regime of systemic oppression and
domination by one racial group over any other”.
In South Africa the Government implemente d a regime of apartheid with penalties
such as fines, imprisonment, and whippings . In 1960 a large group of black citizens in
Sharpeville refused to carry their passes, and in retaliati on the Government declared a
state of emergency for 156 days, leavi ng 69 people dead and 187 wounded. Thousands
of individuals died in custody, frequently af ter gruesome acts of torture. How, then,
does this crime against humanity apply to the introduction of Whānau Ora?
Whānau Ora is about empowering and enabling families to set their own priorities to
focus on outcomes. Common themes in w’ ānau plans include better  lives for children,
employment, housing and homeownership, ed ucation and skills development, and
health and cultural wellness. Presumably, this is the nature of what Mr Peters labelled
sociological objectives, whic h are of no interest to M āoridom at all. Although it is
pleasing to note that  in a different waka Mr Cunliffe st ated that he would listen to the
voices of M āoridom as to where they want to take Wh ānau Ora, in the next breath he
admitted that he would not be keeping th e policy going as it is, suggesting that Wh ānau
Ora is not something Labour would limit to M āori and that Labour wants to extend it to
community service agencies and NGOs around the country.
This too must be challenged. Wh ānau Ora is available to any family—any family—
who wants to support and accept responsibilitie s and obligations to one another. The
days are gone when progress is measured by wh at others do to families in the name of
development. Wh ānau Ora is not about being done to, or being on behalf of, others.
Whānau Ora, contrary to the view above, has been openly embraced by New Zealanders
of all cultures and creeds and is about families standing confidently and being capable
of taking care of their own. Call it transf ormation. Call it liberation. This is about a
revolution of the masses to set their own direc tion. I really im plore our political
colleagues to think seriously before they jump in and attack merely for the sake of
gaining traction on the hustings.
I would ask this House to think back to the debates around section 59 of the Crimes
Act, where the use of violence as a mean s of disciplining children was outlawed, or,
more recently, in the wonderful coalition of minds that came together for tobacco
reform to ensure improved health outcome s for all New Zealanders. Both of these
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15543
policy initiatives were championed by activists, lobbyists, health professionals, families,
children’s advocates, academics, and communitie s. They came together to mobilise the
masses in the interest of change. So when I look at the 160 providers  that have entered
into Wh ānau Ora and, most important, the 33,000 New Zealanders who have been
touched by the impact of positive approaches for w’ ānau and families, I know that we
are observing a new form of political activism, driven by results and by widely felt
support.
When people attempt to denigrate their effo rts or think they can look from afar and
want to meddle in the lives of participati ng families who have worked so hard to build
their collective capacity, it makes no sense to me. These same people, who for years
have created dependence on the State, cannot th ink that people can restore self-belief in
what they can do for themselves. Our efforts th is year will continue to strive for the
highest results to make the lives of New Zealand families and w’ ānau better. We will
not resile from that pursuit of excellence at  every encounter our families have with the
State.
I for one fully support the Government’s mission of five out of five children
succeeding in schools. I have no tolerance for accepting mediocrity when the future of
our children is at stake, but I do not believe that simply pouring more personnel into the
school grounds will necessarily bring the results. A chorus line of sc hool nurses, social
workers, cafeteria caterers, and the like will not make the difference we need, unless we
actively enable our families to be in charge of supporting their children in their
educational pathways. The M āori Party has consistently spoken up about the key
priority to address income disparity, and we  are relentless in our  call for Government,
business, and the private sector to take seriously the campaign for a living wage.
Finally, I want to address the myth-making that is associated with our role as a
partner in Government. Our founding presid ent, matua Whatarangi Winiata, always
challenged the members of the M āori Party to lift our sights high, to do everything
possible to herald improveme nts for all those who call Ao tearoa home. Our current
president, Naida Glavish, has continued this  theme with a message that the days of
doing the haka outside the fence are over. We have an absolute responsibility to anyone
who places their faith in kaupapa M āori as a framework for this  nation, and we will not
let their aspirations be left to flounder by choosing to sit def eated on the Opposition
benches.
Our reason for being is to apply every mechanism possible towards strengthening our
w’ānau to do for themselves, and I make no apology for the investment that we have
been able to negotiate in a stronger future. I am proud th at through our work we have
achieved an extra $47 million to support trade training places for 3,000 M āori and
Pasifika peoples and an a dditional 400 cadets in the energy, infrastructure, and
telecommunications industries. I am proud th at we fought for an extra $100 million to
insulate homes of low-income households—especially those with children with high
needs—increased resources to reduce rheumatic  fever, a warrant of fitness trial for
Housing New Zealand properties, and 2,000 vege gardens. I am particularly pleased at
the wide range of initiatives that we have  championed to change social attitudes and
increase the participation of disabled peopl es in all aspects of life, and the progress
made in enabling Māori and Pasifika families to confront and address family violence in
their midst, and there is much more. The point is that if our greatest fault is that we have
stepped up to make a difference for our cons tituency by working with this Government,
then so be it.
Returning to R ātana, I want to end by talking about the absolute standout
performance in the R ātana talent quest by a young T ūwharetoa singer called Jackson
Owen, who will in a couple of weeks’ time be  making his way to Florida to start his
15544 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
music career. Jackson was discovered when his w’ ānau uploaded on YouTube tracks of
him singing. If the last 24 hours have told us anything, with backing and support even a
humble schoolgirl can overnight become a two-time Grammy award winner. Would it
not be a great day when our combined efforts could reach across the House to make sure
that every child experiences success, that every w’ ānau knows the meaning of mauriora
in their lives? That is a campaign that I am determined to uphold.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. T ēnā koe
whaea mō tērā kōrero.
[Thank you for that speech, madam.]
Seeing as the Prime Minister may have mi ssed the fact that while he was up in
Hawaii playing golf and his MPs were sizing up more investment properties to buy for
the biggest untaxed capital gains they could get, most Kiwi families were actually going
backwards. Since Parliament last sat, housing has become even less affordable, more
families have fallen behind in their rent, more families have been evicted, more families
have shifted to caravan parks, the price of food and just about  everything else has
continued to rise, more jobs have beco me more precarious and more people have
become poorly paid, more food parcels ha ve been given out at food banks, more
families have had their electricity cut off because they cannot pay the bill, more children
are in hospital with poverty-related illnes ses and diseases, and more children are
regularly going hungry.
Big bank economists tell us we are about to benefit fr om a rock star economy in
2014, but that is rubbish. Everywhere in the world, the benefit of the economic recovery
is going to the richest 1 percent while the 99 percent either stagnate or go backwards,
and New Zealand is no exception. The rich ge t richer and the poor  get poorer under a
system where people strive to get as rich as they can and the wi nner is the person who
has the most money when they die.
How crazy is that? How does that make sense when kids go hungry because families
have to pay the rent, the electricity, the pe trol for the car, doctors’ bills, and medical
bills before they can even afford to buy food for the kids? But does this Government
care? Not for 1 second.
Take loan sharks, for example. Six years a go this Government said it wanted to deal
to loan sharks for preying on poor families. Well, what did it do? Nothing. Instead, it
bailed out the banks, wealthy investors, a nd companies like South Canterbury Finance,
which got a $1.7 billion taxpayer windfall, which in one single gift to the rich was more
than the entire 22 years of Treaty of Waitangi settlements, where iwi ended up with less
than 3 percent of what was stolen from them . Meanwhile, the victims of loan sharks are
told that they have to pay up to 500-plus percent interest rates so that a small loan to pay
a power bill rapidly becomes a crippling debt to the loan sharks, with no bailouts for the
poor.
Housing is the same. Everyone knows that  housing is becoming less affordable.
Mortgages are through the roof, and as intere st rates go up—it was in the paper this
morning—so do rents. But this Government has no plans to create more affordable
housing for low-income families who need them the most. In Glen Innes and elsewhere,
the Government is actually pushing people o ff the waiting list, then telling everybody
that State houses are no longer needed, a nd then bulldozing those homes so private
developers can build mansions for the rich.
In education, the Government is also missing the mark. Instead of ensuring that every
child can learn by adopting a comprehe nsive food in schools programme, as
recommended by its own experts, it is focusing on a failed charter schools model from
overseas and drop-in principals. We have all heard the drivel about how poverty has
nothing to do with educational underachievement , but that is a refrai n delivered only by
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15545
those commentators who choose not to hear the advice and Governments that choose to
ignore the inequality that is at the heart of increased so cial problems in low-income
communities.
As for those jobs, Mr Key, are you happy th at unemployment help s to keep wages
down and to keep workers worryi ng that they might lose their jobs? Is it your  plan that
260,000 workers cannot get a job or cannot ge t enough hours at work to pay for a
decent chance in life for themselves and thei r families? Is it your plan that this
Government has no policy at al l to create meaningful empl oyment, except to leave the
fate of the worker in the hands of the fr ee market? Instead, all we get is policy after
policy, bill after bill, to take even more fr om low-income workers—employment rights,
social support, tax dollars,  and all of that—to feed oi l and mining giants, property
developers, foreign bankers, casino bosses, private consultants, and the like.
Families are struggling—M āori families, Pasifika families, and increasingly more
Pākehā families—after decades of the deepest cuts this country has ever experienced.
These cuts come from policie s that have deliberately driven hundreds of thousands of
families into poverty, policies that have led us to a direction that has been disastrous for
all Kiwi families outside of the comfortable middle class and ruling elite, and a
direction that has brought us to a critical  crossroads in our lives. There is growing
inequality, homelessness, and unemploymen t, and a growing population of working
poor who cannot even make ends meet.
At the end of the last year, the worl d mourned the loss of Nelson Mandela and
celebrated his momentous life. But Mandela wa s not just an anti-apartheid campaigner;
he was also a fighter for the poor who once said: “Overcoming poverty is not a task of
charity; it is an act of justic e. Like slavery and apartheid, poverty is not natural. It is
man-made and it can be overcome and eradicated by the actions of human beings.”
Mandela considered poverty to be one of the great evils of  the world and believed there
could be no freedom where poverty persists.
At the beginning of this new year, Mana stan ds resolute in our determination to find
ways to eradicate poverty—particularly child poverty—wherever and however it may
exist. We will do all we can to ensure that  this issue is the issue by which political
parties are measured by voters in 2014. Mana  wants a new deal for Aotearoa—one
based on everyone playing their part and everyone paying their way, not just families
but Government and big business as well—and an economy where everyone can live in
dignity and respect and where jobs are secu re, hard work is rewarded, and people can
earn enough to give their families a decent standard of living.
Mana is calling for homes for every Ki wi family—the building of 10,000 homes a
year, especially for those on low incomes—until every child in every family is housed
in a clean and warm home. This will create thousands of jobs in design, architecture,
carpentry, cabinet making, painting, roofi ng, electrical work, pl umbing, drainlaying,
landscaping, roading, community infrastructure, and all the re lated jobs that come with
a strong and vibrant housing sector. Mana will encourage immigrants to build new
homes rather than buy existing ones, to increa se the jobs in the housing sector and to
keep the current housing stock for kiwis. And Mana will introduce a serious capital
gains tax to force those with too many inve stment properties to sell back into the
housing market, drive down the prices, and fr ee up homes for those who can afford to
buy but cannot find anything in the overheated market place.
Mana wants jobs for all and Government -created community work on an index
minimum wage for everyone else who is able to work in hospitals, schools, old people’s
homes, marae, sports clubs, local parks, an d the like, giving pe ople the opportunity to
rebuild their confidence and develop basic work  skills, while helping to revitalise their
communities. Mana wants financing and ment oring for small business, because if you
15546 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
back small-business owners, they commit to a fu ture in this country, rather than leave,
and their success encourages their families to do the same.
Mana also calls for taxing the rich to free the poor, introducing a “Hone Heke tax” on
all financial trans actions, adding billions to the national budget and enabling
Government to launch positive jobs progr ammes, feed the kids, provide a well-
resourced and positive educational environment at all levels, reduce taxes for low-
income earners, and abolish GST on food and essential services. Of  course, Mana also
supports taking back the power. In today’s wo rld, access to a consiste nt and affordable
supply of electricity is a staple part of  life for all New Zeal anders. It was never
envisioned that it be owned by private investors. Mana supports reclaiming all
electricity assets for the benefit of all citizens of Aotearoa.
Mana’s position is clear. This is not a time for ti nkering. This is a time to be bold, to
chart a new path, and to establish a new deal , where a life of dignity and respect is a
birthright afforded to everyone. We call on a ll of the parties to ri se to the challenge
rather than surrender to the squabbling. Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, kia ora tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. The seeds
of my political philosophy lie in my backgr ound. I am not sure how much the previous
speaker, Hone Harawira, knows about child poverty. I know a lot about child poverty. I
know what it is like to live in  a house with no power a nd no running water; having a
bath once a week in a 44-gallon drum cut in half; sleeping on straw covered with sacks;
going to bed every night hungry, piddli ng the bed every night—psychologically
disturbed—and being thrashed every morni ng for piddling the bed every night. I know
what it is like going to school every day in an ex-army uniform with no shoes; spending
all day, every day, out of the classroom stealing other kids’ lunches; going home to
bread and milk—at best—at night , cooked over an open fire w ith sugar on top; if I am
very lucky, taking Weet-bix covered in dripping to school each day; and living in a very
dark hole. That is child poverty.
If I thought that the policies of the prev ious speaker from the Tai Tokerau would
work against that—and they do exist; they do exist—I would go to the other side of the
House and support him. I would be the first to  line up to support him. Why would I not
be the first to line up to support Hone Harawira  if he had the answers to this country’s
deep, deep vein of underprivilege, desperati on, desolation, and desp air that so many of
our kids live under? If I thought that his po licies were the answer , I would line up with
him and I would say so.
But let me give him one ticket out of child poverty that he might like to think about.

items.speaker: That one ticket is twofold
items.text: living in a home with unconditional love—and I never knew
about that—and a world-class education. I did get that—a world-class education. If
every one of his people lived in a home with unconditional love and access to a world-
class education, then in a ge neration we would get rid of the deep vein of social
deprivation and child poverty in this country. That is the ticket. That is the only ticket—
not welfare, not big Governments, not mo re borrowing, and not more handouts. It is
instilling in people that having children is a God-gi ven right but an awesome
responsibility, that love goes a long, long way, and that a world-class education is a
ticket to the future for so many of these pe ople whom the previous speaker talked about
and represents to the best of his ability in this House. But he is misguided.
In a couple of weeks we ar e going to open the first ch arter school—they call it—in
Northland. I do not mind whether they call it a charter school or whether they call them
partnership schools, but this is what I can tell you. The first partnership school in
Whangarei will open in 2 weeks’ time. As a pr ivate provider for the last 4 years it has
taken 40 Māori boys and girls from the poorest, poorest families in the whole of the Tai
Tokerau. It has boarded them in Whangarei, and it has given them an opportunity to go
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15547
to the best State schools in Whangarei, mostly Whangarei Boys High School, and after
school they are tutored. They get in that co llective home unconditional love every day
of the week and tutoring every night of the week. They feel a sense of purpose and
direction.
Those young people sit National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA)
level 1 with a 100 percent pass rate, I say to the Minister of Finance, a 100 percent pass
rate in that partnership school in Whangarei for the last 4 years, a 100 percent pass rate
in NCEA level 1 in Whangarei with M āori boys who come from places that the
previous speaker represents and knows not hing about. The previous speaker has a
doctrine he peddles in this House that is bankrupt—more borrowing, more welfare, and
less responsibility. He does it because he thinks there are votes in it. There are no votes
in representing people who have no hope, and that member will not get up on his hind
legs and say to this House: “I’m going to support the partnership school that has served
my mokopuna in Tai Tokerau fo r so, so long.” That member and the Labour Party have
promised to close down that school, whic h gets a 100 percent—100 percent—pass rate
in NCEA level 1.
That is the ticket out of deprivation. Th at is the only way, th e one-way street, the
only way out of poverty in this country. It will  take a generation, but this is what this
Government is working on. It stands for br inging those people up. It is like high tides
raising all boats. Lift the standards at the bottom and the high tide will rise and raise
more boats—all boats. We have tried th rowing money. We have tried borrowing
money. We have tried big welfare. And what  we do know is that any Government big
enough to give you everything you want is a Government big enough to take from the
hard workers everything they have.
So if we want to deal with the deep ve in of social deprivation—and I do because I
know what it is like, and it is a dark place, a ve ry dark place—then we have to deal with
the fundamentals of human behaviour: taking  responsibility for your family, giving
them unconditional love regardle ss of your status or your w ealth, taking advantage of a
world-class education that is there fo r you at the school down the street, and
encouraging young people to do that. It will be a generation, but it will lift them out. If
we want to empty the jails, we have got to educate the young people. If we want to get
the health lists down, we have got to teach you ng people what it is like to be in charge
of yourself and take responsibility for your own actions. Then we will make progress.
But borrowing from the savings of offshore pe ople to hand out to others in a country
and mounting up the debt to the next generati on is not the way we deal with poverty in
this country.
Of course I support sandwiches and food in schools—by God, I would have loved
some sandwiches and some food in school—but that is not the answer. The answer is
getting the fundamentals of the New Zealand economy so that we are internationally
competitive. I pay tribute to Bill English, whom  I have worked with closely these last 2
years, who has done a remarkable job of tu rning this economy round. I give praise to
the Prime Minister and Cabinet and the National Party caucus—my coalition partners—
for taking tough decisions. The answer to child poverty, I say to the parliamentary
Opposition, is not about taking others’ money and throwing it at a problem, because we
have tried that and it has failed.
The answer is education. The answer is  giving everybody the opportunity of the
dignity of work, and you can have a jo b only if you are educated. And you can get
educated only if you go to school. And you can go to school only if you come from a
home that loves you. And the corollary to th at is a dark place, and I know about living
in dark places. So if we want to deal with  the fundamental issues of about 20 percent of
this country’s young people coming from dysfunc tional homes and families, we have to
15548 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
deal with the causes, not with the political side effects for the purposes of getting a few
votes.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I commend my colleague the
Hon John Banks for his candour, for his cour age, and for his plain speaking in the
House this afternoon. It is a timely reminder to  all of us, as this parliamentary year
starts, about why we are here. Whatever ou r political perspectiv e or our philosophies,
my colleague’s speech has reminded us that, ultimately, the challenge all of us face and
the responsibility we accept is to try to  do good for our fellow New Zealanders through
our service in this House, to make sure that every child gets the best start in life and that
it is more than just a slogan, to make sure that families are valued as the cornerstone of
our society, and to make sure that fr om good, strong families vibrant communities
grow. They will be diverse. They will be different. While we hold, amongst our
differences, the collective view that that is what we are about, our responsibility is to
focus on the issues and to make sure that we make the best fist of what we have got, in
order to achieve those goals for the people we represent.
And it is in that vein that I welcome our two new members who were sworn in today.
I congratulate them on their election to this Parliament, I wish them well for the time
they are here, and I look forward to the c ontribution they will make. If I can offer one
word of advice, it is that when I first became a member of Parliament many years ago,
an elderly predecessor in my seat, the Rt  Hon Sir John Marshall, befriended me and
gave me the advice that when you work on your maiden speech, do it from the
perspective that every few years it is wort h re-reading again to see whether you still
hold true to the values you expressed in that speech. And use that opportunity not just to
tell the electorate at large about you a nd what you stand for but to anchor your
philosophy for the time you will be a member of Parliament. So I wish both those
colleagues well.
Let me turn to the Prime Minister’s stat ement and say how delighted I was both at
the announcement late last ye ar and the reaffirmation in the statement today that the
Transmission Gully motorway north of Wellin gton is to proceed this year. That has
been a critical part of the confidence a nd supply agreement between United Future and
National, it has been part of the Wellington agenda since about 1939 to have a coherent
northern access and egress constructed as an al ternative to what was then the goat track
of Ngauranga Gorge, and it has been some thing that Wellingtonians for generations
have held out there as some mystical thi ng that might one day appear, all the time
having the sinking feeling in their stomachs that it will never happen. That yin and
yang, if you like, of hope and missed opportunity was given a very confident stamp of
approval by the Prime Minister before Ch ristmas, and the peopl e of the Wellington
region look forward with c onfidence to the commenceme nt of work on this long-
overdue project during this year and will be casting their eyes very widely at other
political parties to see what their intentions  are with regard to its continuation and its
development and its completion within the time frame that has been set out.
As recent events—as recent as last Monday—showed in this region, we are
vulnerable to a major seismic event and in that  eventuality our ability to get in and out
of this place with any form of efficiency or  rapidity will be se verely compromised by
the lack of an alternative to the existing access and egress points, so it is a vital part of
our safety and our transport network and it will be very much welcomed by the people
of this region.
Over the last few days the political debate for 2014 has started to take shape around
the issue of what is the best way of delivering what looks like being a period of
Government surplus to the benefit of the families of New Zealand. I am not going to
play politics with some of the solutions that have been proposed, because I think there is
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15549
merit in all of them, but there are also fish -hooks in all of them as well. The critical
point is this: the Government already spends billions of dollars in assistance and support
in various forms for the families of New Zealand. The Working for Families tax credit
scheme is the obvious example. The changes made to personal tax rates, particularly the
bottom two steps, in recent years is another.  We have paid parental leave. We have
various other forms of assistance. If one was to tally up the quantum, one would see that
it is a very large figure, but the questions that the current debate gives rise to are
whether these entitlements are properly and efficiently structured, whether there are too
many anomalies and uncertainties that will be  perpetuated by the types of changes now
being proposed, and whether ther e are alternatives for the delivery of the goal, which I
do not think there is any great disagreement about seeking to achieve.
I note, interestingly enough, that in Mr Cunliffe’s statement yesterday he positioned
his policy around the figure of a household income of $150,000 per annum. Yet there is
already legislation before this House, th e Taxation (Income-sharing Tax Credit) Bill,
that allows households with a joint income of up to $140,0 00 to split their income for
tax purposes. The principal argument that has be en raised against that has been that the
benefit is delivered to those too far up th e income scale—those earning up to $140,000
as a household income. But now it seems acce ptable to pay $60 per child a week to
families earning up to $150,000. I think that highlights some of the dichotomy that I am
speaking about. It would seem to me that a far more logical approach, which would be
not only more efficient in its distribution but actually less costly long term, would be to
proceed with the income-sharing legislation, to restructure the Working for Families tax
credits so that the principal benefit was de livered to families who fall below about the
$70,000 household income mark, who are those w ho would currently benefit least from
a change to income sharing. We could then use the additional fi nance that would be
saved by that move to extend paid parental leave, certainly to 26 weeks and beyond that
ultimately to 52 weeks. We could then look at  moving out from there to take some of
the antenatal moves that were  announced by the Labour Party yesterday as being in its
policy, extend those, and more coherently fund them. And th en we could look also at
the issue of both the provision of medicine s and also early childhood education. We
could then put together an overall integrat ed package using to maximum impact the
totality of the funding currently  available and getting around th e situation that we have
at the moment and its inevitable consequence of a targeted approach, if you like.
But if we take the Labour Party example as just one example of this problem, we see
that at up to $150,000 you are OK, but at $150,001 you fall off the cliff. I am not
blaming the Labour Party particularly for that, but it is always that issue when you come
to drawing the line. I think that what we have with the measures that Labour proposed
yesterday, with the measures that were in the Prime Minister’s state of the nation speech
last week about education, and with some of the measures that the Greens proposed at
the weekend—although I think th ey were largely in our po licy 3 years a go—is that if
we put them altogether, we have the capacity, utilising the finance that is available, to
bring out a coherent, rational, workable sche me that benefits those whom we seek to
assist, and there does not seem to be too much disagreement about who those audiences
are, but which also removes a number of th e boundary traps, the poverty traps, or even
those effective high marginal tax rates that cut in when some of these changes occur. So
I hope that the debate this year is not about  my auction versus your auction, or my bribe
versus your bribe, but about us ing the totality of measures that have been proposed to
bring forward a constructive proposition from which all New Zealand families will
benefit in the future, and that the timely reminder given to the House by my colleague
the member for Epsom just a few moment s ago is one that stays in our minds
15550 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
throughout the year and is one we all seek  to do our very best to deliver upon,
alleviating the conditions that that member so eloquently described.
I say to members in conclusion that it is great to be back this year. I hope that
everyone enjoys the challenges  of the year that lie ahead , and may they all get the
desserts that they deserve, come a certain event later in the year.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Can I start by acknowledging two of
my colleagues. Sam Lotu-Iiga, just the third Pacific member of Parliament to become a
Government Minister, is a man of real capac ity who will benefit not just his community
but New Zealand. I also acknowledge Jo Ha yes, whom the Labour Party members may
not know well but they should understand that  she was the person who helped us win
the party vote in Dunedin South with an excellent campaign on the ground in heartland
Labour territory, increasing the National Part y vote by thousands, and she is a welcome
addition to the caucus—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Even with Clare Curran as her opponent.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Even with Clare Curran as her opponent. Can I also
acknowledge the leadership of  the Prime Minister. I think in his address today he
demonstrated again that his leadership of New Zealand th rough these last 5 or 6 years
has been critical to lifting New Zealande rs’ sense of confidence and aspiration, their
greater sense of self-reliance and resilience, which has seen this country come through
very difficult economic times in about as good a shape as it possibly could, and he has
helped lay a platform for this country and its families to enjoy the benefits of one of the
better-growing economies in the developed world.
What a sharp contrast with the Leader of the Opposition.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, nothing has really cha nged in 12 months with Labour.
Twelve months ago it had an unpopular leader, who was going nowhere, and Grant
Robertson was undermining him, and the same  thing is going on now. Quite apart from
the huge difference in their speeches, the Prime Minister enjoys the support of his
caucus. The Labour caucus is not enjoying Da vid Cunliffe, and that shows up in its
support.
You see, what we heard was a speech about the kind of country and Government that
Labour and David Cunliffe wish they we re campaigning in. They wish income
inequality was growing, but it is not. It is not growing. The facts are clear: the poor are
not falling behind, the middle class is not flat-lining, real incomes are growing, the most
vulnerable have been protected, and income in equality is stable to slightly improving.
But on “Planet Cunliffe” something quite di fferent is happening, or he wishes it was
happening. He wishes he was campaigning against a Government that was hostile to the
most vulnerable, but, of course , it is not. We borrowed billions  of dollars to protect the
most vulnerable through a recession. He wishes there was no innovation in the
economy, but, in fact, we are seeing a blossoming of New Zealand’s IT and
manufacturing sectors, public floats, international deals—you name it. He wishes there
was a manufacturing crisis—what happened to  that inquiry—but ther e is not. In fact,
because those members declared a crisis, ma nufacturing started doi ng well. He wishes
the regions were weak, but, actually, the data  shows very clearly that the regions are
doing better than the metropolitan areas—again, because Labour declared that they were
doing poorly. He wishes that public confidence was on its knees, but it is not. More
New Zealanders believe more positively in the aspirational future of this country than at
any other time I can remember in 25 years of  public life, and they know that it has got a
solid basis.
But on “Planet Cunliffe” there is no confidence. People are fearful. People have no
hope. And you can hear it, can you not? He stood in front of the mirror and said that line
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15551
and enjoyed it. But it is just no t true; that is all. It sounds really good; it is just not true.
He wishes that all those people who have traditionally supported the Labour Party in the
social service sector—iwi, churches—and he wi shes that teachers were marching in the
street. And what did they do last week? They applauded the Government’s education
policy in a way that I cannot recall for a Na tional Government in a long time in this
Parliament. Those people, who used to feed  the Labour Party cases  of Public Service
breakdown, are working every da y with this Government a nd its agencies to improve
our communities, to make our communities safer, to lift the achievement of those who
have underachieved, to reduce the reoffendi ng rates of our pris oners, and to reduce
welfare dependency, because the policies of  this Government in those areas are
meritorious, they are thoughtful, they are progressive, and they are working.
So, again, on “Planet Cunliffe” all thos e people would be supporting the Labour
Party. In fact, they might go and vote for it in the booth if Labour can achieve its
brilliant new strategy, which is to get Labour voters to vote Labour. That is the strategy:
get Labour voters to vote Labour. Well, I can tell those members that we are doing a
better job of getting Labour voters to vote Natio nal, and that is why we can go into this
election year with some confidence.
I used to think it was “Planet Labour”, but increasingly I think it is “Planet Cunliffe”.
I think there are two planets now, actually. There is “Planet Labour”, which is still
sitting there pining for the return of He len Clark and Michael Cullen—leaders whom
those members took seriously, and the country  did for a while, too—and then there is
“Planet Cunliffe”, which is a noble and lonely place to be. There is no doubt about that.
It is a noble and lonely place.
It is the “Bad Start” policy that ha s highlighted that gap enormously—the
announcements in the last week or so. David Cunliffe’s policy around payments to
families is based on the idea that he can save $1.5 billion by not pursuing promises he
made that would cost $1.5 billion. At leas t the Greens went to th e trouble of running
their money through the photocopier. On “Planet Cunliffe” you just imagine it. It is like
going into the shop and saying: “It’s a barg ain. I saved money because it was going to
be $200 for the running shoes, but they are on sale at $100. I’ve saved $100, so I can go
and spend it on something else.” The $1.5 billion does not exist in the Government
forecasts, so it is not available for saving, and the media and David Cunliffe and the
Labour Party have figured that out only today.
The other thing that those me mbers have said today is that in order to enforce
international tax obligations on companies like Facebook, they might ban them from
New Zealand. They might ban Facebook from New Zealand. Well, we know that that
works. We know that that works because they  have done it in North Korea and it has
worked there. [ Interruption] Well, there is no income, so they pay no tax. That is how
they do it: get rid of the income and then they get rid of the tax problem.
The Labour Party is dealing with the New Zealand public, who are suspicious of any
cash splash, as we have seen in the last fe w days, but it is too l azy to deal with the
problems that are actually about our most  vulnerable: getting immunisation rates up,
protecting children from violence, a nd lifting educational achievement. The
Government will continue to advance its Business Growth Agenda this year. It will
continue to advance its prudent fiscal management. It will continue to advance a
programme of microeconomic reform to s upport jobs and incomes. Jobs will come
faster and incomes will grow faster under an ongoing National Government. Our
process of considered and consistent cha nge, working closely with the community and
the business community, is starting to yiel d real benefits. Co mmunicating openly and
being accountable for those policies has built real confidence that the National
Government has its finger on the pulse of what  is required, the political will to do what
15552 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
is required, and the leadership to take the public along with it. That  is why we can face
this motion of confidence in Parliament with some real confidence.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I want to begin by acknowledging some of the
contributions that have been made by my colleagues in the House today, particularly the
personal address that was made by the Hon John Banks, and to just again articulate that,
of course, when we discuss issues of poverty, we often also discuss at times issues of
neglect. But they are in some cases two ve ry different things, and we have always
required different policy respons es to address those issues. No one has ever argued that
those issues are simple. They are complex and require not just one response but multiple
responses, and I will speak today to some of Labour’s ideas in that area.
State of the nation speeches, as we have seen in the past 2 weeks, speak volumes
about the vision and direction that  political parties want to ta ke not just their parties in
but voters—indeed, the entire  country—in the future if they are the successful
Government after an election. You can see where there is commonality and you can see
where there is a very big difference. You can see where there is consensus and where
there still remains debate. If you want to talk  currently about areas of consensus, it is
very hard to argue that not all of us want  children to have a good education in this
country. In fact, we want children—no matte r which school they go to, no matter which
community they grow up in—to have the best education po ssible. There is absolute
consensus on that. That is why you saw Labour respond to even the Government’s
package as having some good ideas that we think we could use. We acknowledged that
because of course we are always trying to  ensure that we have good professional
development and support for our schools. We can quibble over details, but that principle
remains. That is why you will have seen us supporting, in the area of education, the
Greens’ ideas. Community hubs are fant astic. The ideas around nutrition in schools—
good stuff. Of course we are in support of that ; in fact, we had similar ideas in our 2011
policy.
But where there continues to be division is  the idea of whether or not children can
have their entire lives turned round by the experience they have once they walk through
the school gate. Can a child leave behind their home life, their upbringing, the nurturing
they have or do not have, whether they have got enough resource, and whether there is a
computer in the home to do their homew ork with, enough money for a school uniform,
or money to participate in school trips? We  can throw all the in-kind assistance in the
world that we want to to families, but if families do not have the resources they need to
do the job that is there, we will always ha ve this debate. In ki nd goes only so far, and
that is why the recent OECD report, the Programme for International Student
Assessment statistics—the ones we all de bated about why we are going backwards—
pointed out that New Zealand and Chinese Ta ipei are standout countries when it comes
to the fact that we have not been able to  overcome those inequalities in our education
system and that perhaps it was time to st art looking at socio-ec onomic factors. The
OECD spelt it out for us. New Zealand would benefit by looking at policies that would
improve the socio-economic status of the children who are currently failing in our
education system.
You cannot isolate a child’s life. You cannot simply fix everything through a teacher,
and nor should we ask teachers to fix everyt hing. So that is why we are looking beyond
that. And why should we look beyond that? Because, quite simply, the cost of families
not having enough to provide for their children costs us mo ney. We spend an estimated
$6 billion per annum on the unnecessary cost  of things like health care—picking up a
child in a hospital system because the fam ily could not afford their prescription or
doctor’s costs. You may argue that under-sixes are free, but I can guarantee that a parent
does not take their child to the doctor for thei r free doctor’s visit if they have got a bill
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15553
that they did not pay when they last visi ted. We know that that  is happening in our
communities.
Those are the kinds of costs we can save if families have the resource they need to do
their own job that they want to  be doing for themselves. It is  not just a waste of money;
it is a waste of human potential. So, as much  as National stands up and says that we
cannot afford to invest, we say that we ca nnot afford not to. We need the political
courage to do it early, to do it at a time when it will take 9, 10, 12 years to start seeing
some of the benefits of what we are proposing now. But it is not about political brownie
points. It is not about these bribes that somehow doing the ri ght thing is all about. It is
about actually getting the outcomes that we ne ed further down the track. When Labour
brings these policies in, I can guarantee that th ere will be a whole lot of political parties
that benefit down the track when our pris on numbers drop and when we start having
preventable hospitalisations drop. It is not about point-scoring ; it is about doing what is
good for New Zealand.
Also, when the Government says that there is not enough money in the kitty to do
this, well, there apparently is enough m oney to spend $40 million on private schools.
That is how much this Government has sp ent. There is enough money to spend over $1
billion on tax cuts to the very people it is now saying are far too ri ch to get anywhere
near close to any kind of support when they ha ve a first child, but they can benefit from
a tax cut from the National Government. There is enough money for those things, but
there apparently is not enough money to invest in childre n. There is enough money to
ignore that we are spending an extraordinary amount on our  universal superannuation
scheme without looking at whether or not we need to start l ooking at the age of
eligibility, not only to guarantee that it remain s universal and that it remains sustainable
but so that we are able to st art investing in children in their youngest years and not just
in our older generation. Both groups deserve our attention as politicians.
But I want to talk in more detail about the Best Start programme because some of the
members on that side of the House seem to have missed the point and the savings that
can be made through this kind  of investment. First, starti ng with the Expert Advisory
Group on Solutions to Child Poverty, the Children’s Commissioner led this group.
Business New Zealand was a member of this group. Even Business New Zealand
acknowledges that businesses are going to su ffer if their future workforce is not
properly supported. Not even Bill English seems to have acknowledged that point that it
has strongly made. Business New Zealand wa s a member of the advisory group that
recommended that New Zealand return to a universal family benefit. We had one. We
had one for many, many years. Many members of this House grew up in families that
received a universal family benefit. In fact , most members of this  House did, because it
was cancelled only in 1991, under Ruth Richar dson. So most of us in this House
benefited from that. It went to a mother primarily and it benefited children. It was a
great part of our system. The expert adviso ry group recommended that we go back to
that—that we return to a universal payment up to the age of 5. Labour has committed to
bringing it in in year 1. There is  no year that you can more justify than the first year for
having such a near-universal payment. We say “near” because we did decide to put a
cap in. We wanted to reach as many families as possible, and this payment will, but we
did decide that in these part icular times we needed to pu t a cap in place. The expert
advisory group said to go even further than we have, but we wanted to put in place the
building blocks for a system that acknowledges that we need step change. We need to
acknowledge that from 0 to 3 is not only th e most important developmental stage for a
child; it is also the portion of time that is the hardest for parents to juggle care and work
in. Those are the years that we need to be supporting, and that is exactly what we will
do.
15554 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
The one thing that that side of the House refuses to ackno wledge, as well, is that 60
percent of people do not get paid parental leav e. Sixty percent of people are not eligible
for paid parental leave. At the moment, what can they do? Oh, maybe there is the
parental tax credit that Jenny Shipley chucked in just so that it would try to be a little bit
of a sop to the people who missed out on paid parental leave. We need something that
acknowledges that the vast majo rity of our families are not eligible for something that
has broad support in this Hous e. So why is there not broa d support for a payment that
acknowledges that important year in the same way that paid parental leave does but that
goes further, that reaches more people? I w ould like to hear the Mi nister of Finance’s
view on that, given that he seems to have an issue with paid parental leave as well.
The Best Start package is not just about in come. It is about education and it is about
health as well, but, ultimate ly, it is about saying that Ne w Zealand children deserve our
support and that parents deserve our trust an d support for them to do the job that is
theirs. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, it must be
election year.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Really?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, apparently it must be. Labour and the Greens have
already rocked up with nearly three-quarter s of a billion dollars a year of spending
ideas, and it is not even the end of January. It  must be election year . As reliable as at
any other time in this House, the Greens and Labour together want to spend your money
before you have even made it, which is remarkably similar to how they have spent their
lives, historically. Once again, we have not ev en managed to get to surplus yet and they
are casting around, trying to spend billions of  dollars. Why do I say billions? Because it
is three-quarters of a billion, and we are not even at the en d of January in an election
year yet.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: They’re going to find oil.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is like the global financia l crisis—well, no, they are not,
not with the Greens. There will not be any oil. There will not be any milk for that matter
either. It is like the global financial cris is never happened. Labour’s last big spending
splurges were between 2005 and 2008. It dramatically increa sed the deficit. Remember
the decade of deficits it left because the music was never going to stop? It dramatically
increased interest costs for New Zealanders, and it put the New Zealand economy into a
premature recession, and it is like that never happened.
That is the trouble with this  Opposition, and Bill Englis h touched on that. There is
this wilful denial to learn anything at all from its period in Opposition, a wilful denial to
actually learn a single thing. I act ually think that it is quite conceited. It was thrown out
once in 2008, but also in 2011 it was rejected  again, and it comes back with the same
old policies in 2014, looking for the same old smack-round Labour has not learnt a
single thing in Opposition.
Mr Cunliffe actually adds another dimension to it, because he is a bit tricky. He is a
bit tricky, our friend Mr Cunliffe, and the jour nalists are working it out. Last week Mr

items.speaker: Cunliffe was there saying
items.text: “Oh, look, I have just saved $1.5 billion a year, so I am off to
spend it all, everybody. It is  all wonderful. So I have cancelled these policies. I now
have a cheque that I can write out for $1.5 billion a year.” And some of the scribes
gleefully reported that that wa s indeed the case—that clever Mr Cunliffe had saved us
$1.5 billion a year and he would now go off and spend it.
Except it was never there—except it was never in the country’s accounts. There was
nothing about GST off fruit and vegetables going out in Treasury projections for the
next 4 years. There was absolutely not hing about the tax-free threshold. But Mr
Cunliffe, by cancelling something that neve r previously existed, has suddenly found
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15555
himself $1.5 billion a year. And now he says: “Oh, but that is  to do with last election’s
costings of our economic plan.” Well, we know  how that ended. Those costings in 2011
sunk Phil Goff when he could not show us the money in 2011. Whos e projections were
they? David Cunliffe’s projections. So Mr Cunliffe is back, except this time he is knee-
capping himself. He should have thought that through.
The reality is that he has no idea how this “Bad Start” package is going to work. And
I say “Bad Start” package because you could not get a worse start to an election year
than an Opposition leader who firstly trips himself up over the way that his package is
going to work—and I understand he is still doin g that as we speak; the package is being
redesigned minute by minute—but who also has no answer to the question about how
he is going to pay for it. That is the tricki ness of Mr Cunliffe, because he is basically
saying: “Everybody, you can have everything that  is being done now and, yes, probably
some of the Green Party stuff as well—including that nice bit that it did yesterday—and
you can have the $600 million and it will all be sweet.” So says the Leader of the
Opposition. Well, he is wrong. It is not sweet. It was not sweet in 2008 after 9 years of
progressively worse policies that were about spending more money than the country had
made, and it is not sweet to go back to it today. The real answer to lifting Kiwi incomes
is attracting investment that boosts jobs. And that is what this National Government is
doing.
That is another thing—Mr Cunliffe is Rip Van Winkle on the economy as well. He
has gone to sleep in 2008 and turned up with the same arguments for business growth in
2014. He says that we should not be expor ting lamb carcasses overseas. We do not—98
percent of New Zealand’s lamb carcasses ar e processed in this country. Wake up, Mr
Cunliffe. Life has moved on. He says that we should innovate. We do innovate. We are
spending $566 million over 4 years to innova tive New Zealand companies, and New
Zealand’s information and communications  high-tech and medium high - tech
manufacturing industry is growin g up like that, and is about to get to the point where it
is already nearly half of our dairy industry exports. That is the reality.
By the way, before Mr Cunliffe gets in with the Greens and tries to shoot it down,
dairy is only 20 percent today of New Zeala nd’s total exports of goods and services. So
here we are doing the things that old Ri p Van Winkle over there has woken up to and
said: “My gosh, it would be a good idea if we actually exported something else besides
meat carcasses.” He needs to do his homewor k. That is the conceit of the Labour Party.
It went out of office and it ha s come back today with the same prescription for 2014 as
it had in 2008 and 2011. It has not learnt anything. It has no t bothered to check what is
going on today, which is also conceited. Meanwhile, the New Zealand economy is
growing strongly, New Zealand confidence is growing, and the public of New Zealand
know that the way to become successful is  to keep doing the things that this
Government has New Zealand doing.
That is the focus that this Government has and we have the greatest level of
confidence since the 1990s. We have one of the greatest le vels of growth across the
OECD, and it is likely to continue. It is not nirvana yet, but if you give us another 3
years, you never know how far you will get. But what you do know with the Labour
Party is that you go backwards to a bunch of failed and rejected policies—policies that
were rejected in 2008 and rejected again in 2011. What we do need to do is continue on
the considered, sensible, conservative path, where we understa nd that there is a balance
between spending and people’s incomes. We understand that you actually have to
reward people for their own hard work and you have to trust them with their incomes to
make good decisions. Those are the sorts of things that you have to do. And you have to
do good public services.
15556 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
I was bemused to see another one, Jacinda  Ardern, up there before, going on about
how they will get prison popul ations down. Well, hello, we have done that. While she
was not looking, in 2008 we inherited a prison population projection that was going up
like this. Now it is going down like that, and crime levels are at record lows.
Meanwhile, Jacinda has picked up the 2008 elec tion plan and says: “Oh, we had better
protest about the state of the prisons and how too many people are going to be in the
prisons.” Believe me, these people in the La bour Party need to upda te what they know.
Sadly, I do not know what they have been doing  in the last 5 years, but they have not
been updating their knowledge at all, they have not been le arning what is happening in
the world today, and they have not been learning what is working.
This Government has been getting on with  the job of improving public services and
of delivering far better results  than Labour ever managed with its avalanches of money.
This Government is getting on with building a strong, competitive economy that
supports and encourages investments and comp etitive Kiwi businesses; getting on with,
frankly, balancing the books, ge tting rid of the decade of deficits, and getting New
Zealand into a position where we can have a strong economic future in this country;
and, above all, getting on with rebuilding our second-largest city.
Yes, we get an economic benefit of th at—this country does—but, by goodness, we
got the economic pain of that in 2010 and 2011. For Mr Cunliffe, in his conceited
manner, to wander around and say that you should discount the growth of
Christchurch—well, that basically involves discounting the pain that Christchurch went
through as well, and we cannot do that. So, yes, there is some benefit in that, but if he
thinks that it is about a milk and Christc hurch story, then, frankl y, he is damning the
efforts of many New Zealand businesses up and down the country that are competing
and succeeding on the world stage.
This Government supports those people. It  is providing a platform for growth and
competitiveness from this little country at  the bottom of the Pacific. The Opposition
needs to wake up and decide it needs a new song.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The Green Party will split its call. There will be a 4-
minute bell.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Happy New Year to you, Mr Deputy Speaker. It is just a
shame that we had to start the parliamentar y year with such a disappointing statement
from the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Oh, come on.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: That is what I thought too. In my area, in health, we had a
statement that the Government was going to focus on prevention—well, that would be a
total reversal of the strategic direction it has followed for 5 years. There is going to be
more of the same in elective surgery, an area that the Governme nt has generally put
more money in to at the expense of everythi ng else in the health sector, but, actually,
because of the focus on numbers, we see thos e with the greatest need often still missing
out because their surgery re quires more time or complexity. We are going to see ACC
levies come down. The Prime Minister failed  to point out that it was, in fact, his
Government that unnecessarily put levies up in the first place.
More generally, we saw more “short-termism”, more 19 th century thinking, more
lack of vision, more lack of hope, and no im agination. We saw more sacrifice of the
environment to further intensify already ove rly dangerously intens ified industries. We
saw more driving of wages and conditions dow n so that ordinary people more and more
serve the interests of a few. For most Ne w Zealanders, it truly is becoming someone
else’s country.
The Green Party offers something different. We bring an understanding that although
what individuals can do by themselves is im portant, if we actually want to transform
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15557
outcomes across all of the areas that matter to people, then the Government needs to be
vitally concerned with whole communities, whole systems, and the linkages between
sectors. We are focused on good lives and a fair future for everyone, in contrast to
policies that drive inequalitie s wider. We are focused on a sustainable relationship with
our natural environment and a clean, green economy that helps us  all deliver on our
social and environmental goals and that does not just exist as an end in itself.
It has been interesting to watch over the past 5 years National members’ tactics in the
general debate each week, b ecause it tells us what their smear tactics are going to be
against us in any given week. The increasing de speration is instructiv e. First of all, we
had the devil beast. Remember that? I guess that is a hard line to maintain nowadays
when National is increasingly reliant on John Banks, Peter Dunne , and the entirely
untested Conservative Party, leaving us to  wonder what rough beast it is that is
slouching its way towards electi on day this year. Then we we re described as the “party
of no” because we said no to all of the National Party’s ideas. Well, it is no surprise that
our philosophy is fundamentally different from  National’s. So, yes, we disagree with a
lot of its ideas, just as it disagrees with a lot of ours.
But it is very interesting to me that when at the beginning of this term of Parliament
the Green Party pointed out to National page s and pages of areas where our policy and
National’s coincided and where we could colla borate, National said no to all of that.
The context for that is that we have b een working together with National under a
memorandum of understanding for 5 years on wa rm, healthy homes; toxic sites, which
my colleague will speak about; resetting trap s; and the area that I have been working
with the Prime Minister on, which is Ng ā Haerenga, the New Zealand Cycle Trail
network. I welcome his comment in the st atement about the opening of new cycle
tracks. I will be standing alongside him, celebrating a resource that brings economic,
environmental, and social benefits to communities around the country.
Ours is a party that is based on values and on a charter. They give us an anchor that
provides us with a stable direction over many years. We understand that New
Zealanders want us to work together with others. We unders tand that they want us to
provide practical, evidence-based, and creative solutions to the problems that our nation
faces in the long term. We are a party that is ready for the election. Bring it on.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker. T ēnā
koutou e te Whare P āremata. It is great to be starti ng the year on such a positive note.
That positive note is that this  is the year when people have  the opportunity to vote for a
party committed to positive solutions. The Green Party is looking forward to engaging
with all New Zealanders about a smart a nd sustainable economy and a compassionate
economy, with strategies that will actual ly reduce inequality and protect the
environment, because the environment is what  sustains everything and everyone in this
country. It is just the Government that has not understood that yet.
Today the Prime Minister’s statement was a little bit of a cheap shot. It is the kind of
thing that Lorde was talking about in her song when she said that the privileged live at a
particular level but the rest of  us do not live there and we  actually do not want to. The
Prime Minister had a number of cheap s hots against the Green s, including a highly
selective interpretation of th e economic situation, where he took credit for all kinds of
things that no one in this H ouse can take credit for and he  skipped over the difficult
issues like climate change; the causes and effects of poverty, unemployment, and under-
employment on people; children’s needs;  and the ever-degrading state of our
environment.
The Prime Minister’s written speech had a focus on natural resources, which really
continued that “mine it, drill it, kill it” ag enda, and conveniently failed to mention some
of the MMP collaborations that have made real change. This is possibly because, as my
15558 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
colleague Kevin Hague has just said, the Government does not want to undermine its
own rhetorical attacks on the Green Party by talking about joint achievements where we
have played a leading and positive role. An example of this is the memorandum of
understanding that I ne gotiated with Dr Nick Smith, and then with Amy Adams, on
cleaning up toxic sites. It is kind of hard to characterise the Green Party members as a
bunch of fringe crazies when we have mana ged to work with Ministers and actually
deliver some very positive changes and lead ership on issues of significant public and
environmental risk.
I was a reluctant participant in the contaminated sites memorandum of understanding
at first, because I was not sure what we would be able to nego tiate. I have been
characterised by the right-wing commentator s who do not know what is going on in
politics as someone who might be a bit too challenging to work with on these things.
But, in fact, despite the changes to the Mini sters and the Government’s instability in the
Government team, we have made some  solid and importan t progress on toxic
chemicals, which will benefit all New Zealanders. The clean-up of the T ūī Mine was an
urgent task, and now the Greens, the local au thority, the Minister for the Environment,
and mana whenua have overseen the clean-u p of the unstable ta ilings dam and an
improvement of water quality from that abandoned mine. We have negotiated a national
register of contaminated sites, and we ar e collectively engaging w ith regional councils
on issues of consistency, recording, and transparency.
These are all going to benef it the environment and people. This is a matter of public
health and the health of the environmen t. I look forward to working with the
Government further on this and to being part  of a new progressive Government to also
work on this in the future, to make sure that we clean up the mess of previous bad
practice and weak regulation, as well as the frightening ignorance around chemicals.
The clean-up of our country is a Treaty issue, and it is the responsibility of all political
parties to make it work. The opportunity of MMP, as Russel Norman said today, is to
get good things done without compromising our principles and our values. So I look
forward to more solid and constructive work on the contaminated sites issue.
The Green Party has also started the ye ar with an excellent policy launch for
reducing inequality through e ducation, which the Prime Minister dismissed as giving
the odd kid a lunch. This particularly unf ortunate disparagement is completely
inaccurate because, in fact, this programme has been well received by many groups
outside this Parliament. Groups such as the Youth Hub Barbadoes in Christchurch said
it was excellent and right on the button because it will help decile 1 to decile 4 schools
give children a lunch, and it also provides an opt in for other schools where children
need to eat to learn. Y ou cannot learn if you cannot eat—food for thought, Prime
Minister. It is very typical of the Greens that we have t hought it through. First things
first, let us make sure our kids are fed, then we can improve the quality of their learning.
We have a very positive and necessary vision that we offer to this country, and a very
green Parliament is what we actually nee d. So when it comes to attacking the Green
Party, as Kevin Hague just said, we have made many positive changes in this term of
Government. Despite the disparagement, attacks, and opposition, we have worked with
Ministers. Despite National ha ving amnesia about that, we  look forward to leading a
progressive Government that will actually  make change on many of these issues.
Whether it is education, whether it is cycleways, whether it is unemployment, whether it
is union rights—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Mr Deputy Speaker, t ēnā koe.
Otirā, tēnā koutou, tēnā tatou katoa huri noa i tō tātou Whare i tēnei tau hou.
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15559
[Greetings indeed to you collectively and to us all througho ut our House in this New
Year.]
I would like to join in the congratulations to our colleague Pese ta Sam Lotu-Iiga on
becoming a Minister, the Minister of Pacific Island Affairs. I look forward to working
with him in carrying on our Government’s commitment to ensuring that Pasifika
communities are recognised for the contribution they make to our country and that they
have the opportunity to grow and streng then that contribution over time through
education and through other investments.
I would also like to acknowledge Jo Hayes. Tēnā koe, Jo. Kei te tū whakahīhī a Ngati
Porou i tō hou mai ki roto i tēnei Whare o tātou.
[Greetings to you, Jo. Ngati Porou stands proud because of your arrival in this
House of ours.]
I acknowledge those members’ competency an d hard work and the fact that they
reflect the diversity and strength of this Na tional Government and its ability to speak to
communities up and down our country.
Our Government has an effective, successf ul, and sustainable education plan. Our
education plan is comprehensive. It focuses on raising achievement for five out of five.
It values the voices and aspi rations of parents, and it is  devoted to strengthening,
recognising, and celebrating the profession wh ile also using taxpayer funds to wisely
invest in infrastructure, a modern learning environment,  and digital technology. We
want every New Zealand child to get a better education so they can be successful here at
home in New Zealand, as well as globally competitive, whether based here in New
Zealand or working overseas.
A quality education and relevant skills are the sustainable answer to hardship and
poverty. We have a very, very good educa tion system. That has not happened by
accident, and nor will it continue without atte ntion. It is successful for most, with our
best students being right up there with th e best in the world, but it has not been
successful for all, and we are focused on en suring that we lift up those who have been
falling behind, while also pushing those who are doing well to do even better.
The evidence is clear. The two in-school f actors that have the greatest effect on
raising achievement are the quality of teach ing and the quality of leadership. The major
new investment that the Prime Minister announc ed last week reflects this best evidence.
It also follows the best practice in the education systems around the world that are
confronting and beating the challenge of delivering equity and excellence—in other
words, that all children get a great education in their education system. It is what our
education professionals are telling us and telling me when I am in schools almost every
week of the school year.
Our Government has invested the most ev er, with $9.7 billion this  financial year—a
40 percent increase over the past 5 years—going  into Vote Education. That has been in
the toughest times. Over and above that, desp ite those challenges, our Government is
investing an additional $359 million over 4 y ears because we are backing the evidence,
backing what works, and backing our teachers and principals to raise the achievement of
all New Zealand children. We are resourci ng collaboration within, between, and across
