schools; creating career pathways that give teachers and principals  further and better
professional options; raising the status a nd profile of the profession; and keeping,
growing, and attracting the best and brightes t into it. That is what our new major
education investment is built and funded to deliver, and we will work with the
profession to ensure that we have the design right so that we can meet the achievement
challenges of ensuring that fi ve out of five of our ch ildren and young people can be
successful at school, and that we get them on to a pathway to realising their potential
and living the lives they want for themselves and their families.
15560 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
We are investing in 250 executive principals who will work with, support, mentor,
and lead a community of schools; 1,000 expe rt teachers who will work with that
community of schools, whose teaching pract ice, quality learning, and rich, deep, and
engaging curriculum knowledge and practice will be shared with a range of schools;
5,000 lead teachers with exemplary classroom pr actice who are willing to share this in
open classrooms so that other teachers can learn from that practice and take it back into
their schools; and 100 change principals who can go into the schools that are struggling
the most, those of highest need, and turn those schools round.
These will not be compulsory appointments. They will not be parachuted in. They
will not be unfamiliar with the culture of our  smaller schools. They will be principals
with a proven track record in a dive rse range of schools who understand the many
inputs that are important to making a school successful for all of those children. Those
principals can be appointed to schools only where there have been vacancies and where
the board of trustees opts in  to the conditions. If they do so, then we are making an
allowance of $50,000 per year, on top of an exis ting salary, for those boards to be able
to appoint those principals.
In addition, we have established a $10 million teacher-led innovation fund. We know
from the best evidence that professionals lear n best from each other and they learn best
where they are operating in situations that ar e practical and realistic and that they face
every day. We know that there are outstanding teachers and principals in our education
system, and we want to make sure that their best practice can become common practice.
This major new investment of $359 million is  part of a quality teaching agenda that
is already well in progress under our Governme nt. It includes a mini sterial cross-sector
forum, which engages leaders from 30 peak  bodies, professional and unions, iwi and
Pasifika, academics, and business people. In  that forum, many ideas are challenged,
interrogated, and often adopted. We are engaged in transforming the New Zealand
Teachers Council into a 21 st century body that will meet the needs of 21 st century
teaching and learning challenges. We propose to introduce legislation to give effect to
that. We are lifting the standard of entry and quality of initial teacher education by
introducing this year new postgraduate quali fications. We are reviewing professional
learning and development for the compulsory school sector. We are reviewing the
regulations, or are about to review the regulations, under the Education Act 1989 to free
up the operating environment so that teach ers and principals can get shot of the
compliance and constraints that really do not make very much difference, to create more
room for them to make the magic that they  do in learning situations in our schools
across the country.
We are hosting the international summit of the teaching profession here in
Wellington at the end of Marc h. We expect to host Minist ers of Education from all
around the world. At the same time, we ar e hosting education festivals in Auckland,
Wellington, and Christchurch to hi ghlight school best practice to  each other, to parents,
and to the community, and to celebrate what is happening in our schools. We are having
the inaugural Prime Minister’s Education Excellence Awards in June this year.
All of these together comprise a quality teaching agenda that is all about the
education plan that our Government has. We know that by raising, recognising, and
strengthening the value, prof ile, and status of our educa tion profession, it cannot help
but lead to deploying best-quality teaching pr actice and best-quality leadership practice
across our 2,500 schools, so that all of our children can have the opportunity to succeed,
to have a better education, and to go on to have a better life.
There has been a lot of talk about education in the last couple of weeks. I am very
proud that our Government opened this year with a focus on education and is leading
this debate. It is a debate about education. Many of the other announcements that have
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15561
been made are a debate about social development, and that is appropriate. We are happy
to engage in those debates because we are already doing almost everything that has been
announced in these fresh, new policies by the Opposition parties.
We are focused on education, and this major new investment is part of an overall
education plan that we have been delivering for the past 5 years, and demonstrates the
fresh ideas we have going forward. I am delight ed to participate in the debate on the
Prime Minister’s statement, and we look forw ard to raising achievement for five out of
five New Zealand children and young people.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. Just to take up a
point from Minister Joyce’s contribution to the debate on the Prime Minister’s
statement. He criticised certain Opposition parties, namely the Greens and the Labour
Party, for putting forward policies valued at, according to him, around three-quarters of
a billion dollars. Of course, Mr Joyce ha s completely ignored the fact that his
Government has just stood in this House a nd promised over a bi llion dollars in new
spending, and that the Prime Minister has gone on record as saying that this will grow in
subsequent years. So I am not quite sure how Mr Joyce can throw stones when he is
living in a particular glass house.
I also pick up the fact from the Minister who has just resumed her seat, Hekia Parata,
with regard to the suggestion that the ne w ideas that are being put forward by the
Opposition parties are not new—possibly. I am  not sure whether the Minister of
Education is aware that lead teachers already exist and that lead teachers have actually
been in schools for a good num ber of years, opening their classrooms for new practice.
This might be another situation where the G overnment is going to have to change the
name, in the same way that it change d the name of char ter schools, because
unfortunately the Government was not aware that every school had a charter as well. So
the Government may need to change the name on that policy.
I am going to spend my time talking partic ularly about the education announcements
and the $359 million worth of new money going into New Zealand schools. Nobody
will criticise more money being placed inside  education, as long as it is appropriately
targeted and well spent, and it can actually have proven outcomes. I need to compliment
the National Party spin doctors on the bril liant job they have done on spinning this
announcement in the last week. I liken it to a cupcake with brillia nt icing on it, which
makes you just want to bite into it. Bu t the moment that you do, you realise that
somebody has substituted salt for sugar. This looks great, but when you get down to the
nitty-gritty of this spend, you can see that there is issue upon issue upon issue, and the
New Zealand public and the teachers unions, particularly the New Zealand Post Primary
Teachers Association and the New Zealand Principals’ Federation, need to continue to
have a really close look a nd conversation about what is  being announced in these
policies.
It looks to New Zealand First like another opportunity for divide and rule, and even
within the week since this announcement has been made—or the days since this
announcement has been made—it has caused a wedge between the teachers unions. We
cannot afford as a nation to have the teachers unions, the teachers, the parents of New
Zealand, the boards of trustees, and all thos e who care for true, free, and wide success
criteria in education be manipulated in this  way by spin doctors from this Government.
This is a very similar spin, and it is po ssibly the same company that came up with the
spin that national standards were going to be good for our children and that creating a
single line in the sand that every single New Zealand child had to jump over at the same
moment, in the same year, and in the sa me way was going to  be good for our young
people.
15562 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
This is another cynical attempt by this Govern ment to portray itself as the party that
cares about public education in New Zealand and its quality delivery for our kids. In
reality, these latest announcements are—and th ey have been identified as such by the
Quality Public Education Coalition—nothing more than a banker’s solution, providing
additional top-down expertise, and very highl y paid at that, rather than a workforce
development approach. These policies create an other level of middle managers, such as
in a corporate environment, whose job it is to tell other people what to do. And how will
these executives be identified as using best practice? Why, they are going to be based on
their national standards results, of course. Ev en the Prime Minister has gone on record
as saying that the national standards results are ropy at the least.
But we will fix that, says Minister Pa rata. We will introduce a computer program
where you can enter test and assessment scores for each child, and the computer will
spit you out a result for that  child. You are either at, above, or below the national
standards. That is called the PaCT tool . The PaCT tool was included inside the
announcement that went out with the Minister’s press release. How convenient is that—
how convenient is that? We now do not need teachers who can actually think for
themselves. We do not need teachers who ac tually have a relationship with their
children. We do not need teachers who can use their personal judgment. It is so
annoying when teachers invest themselves person ally inside their children, inside their
students, and inside their classrooms! It is so annoying when those people will not do as
they are told! So we need to develop a way by which we can force those people to do as
they are told. I mean, after all, they are public servants. There is a very good reason why
in most dictatorships the first people that are got rid of ar e the teachers. The first people
a dictator removes are the teachers, because they are the people who think and who truly
care about their young people, a nd provide knowledge, and will not back away from a
confrontation.
This is a trickle-down theor y. This is a trickle-down po licy. This Government has
just repackaged its educational policies from the 1990s. It has possibly got in some new
spin doctors and put a different label on it, but this is trickle-dow n. It is going to put
bonus payments on to a certain numb er—6,700-odd—of our thousands of teaching
professionals, and it is going to make them compete for those positio ns. It is going to
put bonus payments on top of them. It is going to shoot them into other schools to tell
them what to do, and it is going to hope that that trickles down to  the 5-year-olds, 6-
year-olds, and 7-year-olds inside those schools.
This new money could have been used to employ the large number of teaching
graduates who cannot find teaching places insi de this country. It was only in October
2012 that the Ministry of Education went and told three-quarters of the teaching
graduates to go overseas to find work. The mini stry said that it might need them in 20
years’ time or it might need them in 10 years’  time, but it said that unfortunately they
needed to go overseas then. We could have put 9,000 beginning teachers into
classrooms, being mentored right now, today, by experienced, senior teachers. We could
have cut those classes—basically, the class size would have been cut in half—giving
that experienced teacher th e opportunity to take those students who require extra
support, and leave the beginning teacher w ho is under their supervision with the
majority of the class to run those rote or ba sic lessons or classes, and actually expand
that experience base.
We would have futureproofed our education environment, and we know that we need
to. We know that we have an ageing populatio n inside our classes. What is the solution
that this Government is going to come up with—import teachers because we have sent
all our young ones away? There was an opportunity here to use this money to take away
those barriers. Current graduates cannot get th e time in the classroom that they require
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15563
to then become registered, which means th at they cannot then go on and actually fully
participate.
This new money could have funded mandato ry professional development in every
staffroom in New Zealand in the delivery of  Te Kotahitanga. The Minister took issue
with the teachers of New Zealand and said that they did not know how to show respect
to M āori students because they could not pr onounce their names. Yet there is no
solution here. There is no support bei ng offered. Resource teachers of M āori are out
there in New Zealand and nobody knows anything about them. They are on the payroll.
They are out there wanting to help, and they want to support the delivery of Te Reo and
tikanga M āori inside our classrooms. Here was an opportunity to actually bring the
resource teachers of M āori on board with some more m oney, to go and professionally
develop Te Kotahitanga th roughout the country—a progra mme that we know does not
just benefit Māori students; it benefits every student. It is base d on principles of respect
and understanding, on individual education pr ogrammes, and on being the best you can
be—not on meeting that line, but on being the best you can be.
This money could have been used to re view Tomorrow’s Schools. Twenty-five years
on we have ripped bits away and we have chucked in something else. The Minister says
that she values the parental voice. Not a single time in any of these statements is there
any parental voice. Not a single in time in any of these statements has there been any
student voice mentioned. Where are the voi ces of the young peopl e who are actually
inside these institutions? Where is the stude nt voice? Where is th e collaboration with
those parents and those students? Where is the widening of the success criteria, not the
narrowing of them? Lorde actually came to sc hool and recognised at 5 years old, as she
has been quoted, that she l oved singing and music. That was inside a State school. At
13, she won Belmont Idol—inside a State schoo l, supported by State teachers, and with
a wide curriculum. This money was squandered.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: What sort of planet is New
Zealand First on, when the Government annou nces additional money to reward lead
teachers and expert teachers, and New Zealand First describes it as an attack on teachers
and makes analogies with dictatorships around the world?

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: “Planet Winston”.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It truly is on “Planet Winston”.
The contrast today between National, La bour, and the Greens could not be clearer
than from this afternoon’s debate. Prim e Minister John Key has set out a clear,
balanced, and affordable plan for our country—a plan that is about balancing our books.
It is a plan that is about striving for excellence in education. It is a plan about rebuilding
Christchurch and about growing businesses an d more jobs. It is about reducing crime
and improved road safety. It is about making houses more affordable.
Denis O’Rourke: And you haven’t done that either.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is about a Firs t World health system. It is about more
operations, about improving—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I just remind the member
Denis O’Rourke that he cannot bring me into the debate. You cannot say “you” because
it refers to the Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is about better health care for our country. And it is about
sensible, practical environmental policies, which I also want to talk about as Minister of
Conservation.
Labour’s latest leader’s speech shows that Labour has learnt absolutely nothing from
its big spending, its big taxing, and its anti-g rowth time in Government. In that Labour
leader’s address, I did not hear a singl e sentence about how we might grow the
economy. You see, the members opposite are all about spending our wealth, rather than
15564 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
the focus on how we created it. I loved Labou r’s notion of saving, with this dropping of
the dopey idea of removing the GST on food and removing the $5,000 tax-free zone,
saying “Oh, we’ve saved $1.5 billion that we  can now spend on the baby bonus.” Well,
this is like me telling my wi fe that I have decided not to buy the thousand dollar flash
suit, but I am going to spend the thousand dollars on some fancy Gucci shoes—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: And that you’d saved it.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Yes, that is right—and that I have saved it.
I also fret when Labour now tells us that families are in poverty if they are earning
less than $150,000 a year. We are going to have  a baby bonus for a very fertile member
like Jami-Lee Ross, who is expanding his family. Jami-Lee Ross is a wonderful father,
but I am sorry, members on this side of the House do not think that we need a baby
bonus for backbench members of Parliament—actually, aspiring backbench members of
Parliament. We are on track for a surplus by the slimmest of margins and we certainly
do not need handouts of that sort. We will go straight back into deficit and debt—the
pattern of Labour Governments.
Let me challenge Labour’s claim that this  Government has done nothing for those
families that are doing it tough. Well, let me take Labour members through it. This
Government has a very proud record. Take warm and dry homes—in 2013 we
completed our programme of insulating every single State house.
Denis O’Rourke: It was the Greens’ idea, not National’s.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Every one of those 69,000 Stat e houses. For the benefit of
New Zealand First, that was not part of the confidence and supply agreement from 2008
in respect of the Greens; that was about another progr amme, and that was for 300,000
homes that we have insulated. Let us ask the question: in the boom economic times, in
the 9 years in which Labour had its hands on the purse strings, how many homes did it
insulate? Very, very few. That is less than 2 percent of what this Government has done
in far tougher times, and Labour members have  the gall to say it is they who have a
monopoly on caring.
Let us go to another ar ea—child immunisation rates. What were the child
immunisation rates when we came into Govern ment? They were less than 80 percent.
They were comparable with those in Th ird World countries. A nd do you know what?
We now have child immunisa tion rates of above 95 percen t. And do you know what I
really celebrate? Pacific Island and M āori rates of immunisation are now above even
European levels and are some of the best, having gone from some of the worst in the
world. I congratulate Tony Ryall and the hea lth team on what they have done in that
space.
Let us take the Government’s latest efforts on rheumatic fever—giving families
priority for State housing to address that. The strategy that we have worked on, together
with the Māori Party, addressing that Third World disease is  part of our programme for
dealing with disadvantage. Every member in  this House would know that it is a good
principal and a quality teacher who are the real  breaker of poverty—the real breaker of
poverty—and that is why this Government is backing the incentiv es for improving the
quality of our teachers and the quality of our  school leadership. You see, there is not a
monopoly on caring in this House. What there is over there is a party that is hell-bent on
giving a handout, when we on this side are hell-bent on giving a hand up, and that will
long be the case.
I want to talk about housing. Le t us first get the record st raight. All of the measures
of housing affordability show that houses today are more affordable than what they
were after 9 years of the Labour Governme nt. The truth is that house prices doubled
during Labour’s time, interest rates were  over 10 percent when we came into
Government, and that had a really tough im pact on New Zealanders aspiring to own
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15565
their own home. We have got a programme last  year that we have really been getting
momentum on: freeing up land supply with th at Housing Accords and Special Housing
Areas Act. We have already, through that legislation, approved 15,000 new sections in
the city of Auckland, and we now have wo rk under way on accords with Christchurch,
Wellington, the Bay of Plenty, and other communities.
We have got a bill before the House dealing with those infrastructure costs. Actually,
an area that has gone up more than any othe r part of the cost of  the House is those
council development charges, and we are fixi ng that. We have got the work progressing
on the materials’ cost, which is going to be  delivering and bearing fruit this year, the
work on sector productivity, and the work that my colleague Maurice Williamson is
doing on compliance costs. And if there are any of those initiatives that excite me, it is
the online building consent service, which has huge potential to make a difference.
Let us look at the re sults. Last year—here, listen to  this—we built more than 20,000
new homes. That is the most in more than  5 years. That is evidence that this
Government’s housing policies are working. I went back through the statistics. There
was a bigger growth in the number of new houses—a bigger growth in the number of
new houses—from 2012 to 2013 than in any year in history. But it is more than that. We
are committed, this year and next year, to building a thousand extra State houses in both
years—a thousand houses in both years. That is more new St ate houses in more than a
decade, and, as well as that, we are partne ring with the community sector to build
community houses, and we are going to do 300 of those this year. That is the biggest
record ever in terms of growth of the community housing sector.
The last area I want to cover is the Pr ime Minister’s speech about conservation and
the goals for this Government to create a reco rd number of marine reserves this year—a
record number of marine reserves this year . I do have to challenge members of both
parties opposite. It was an extr aordinary comment. They said  that National is allowing
deep-sea drilling without any environmental ru les. That is the claim they have made.
Let us tell the truth—let us tell the truth. The reality is that during the last Labour
Government there was deep-sea drilling with  absolutely no environmental rules in the
exclusive economic zone. It is this Government that has passed that exclusive economic
zone legislation and set up th e Environmental Protection Aut hority to ensure that there
are checks. With the subantarctic islands, w ith Akaroa, with our initiatives on the West
Coast and in Kaik ōura, we are going to be ma king more progress on marine
conservation in any year, again furthering the balanced programme this Government
has.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, can I
first of all wish you a very happy new year and say how much I enjoy it when you are in
the Chair. I would like to respond, before I gi ve my contribution to this debate, to Dr
Smith on one point. Dr Smith, I suggest that you read the article by Professor Graeme
Aitken, the Dean of Education from Au ckland University—someone who, I suppose,
knows a little bit about e ducation—who wrote in the New Zealand Herald  today: “the
Everest of research … shows that socio-econo mic status is the strongest predictor of
achievement.” So maybe, Dr Smith, you might like to start with this.
In April 2011 the Chief Science Advisor to  the Prime Minister, Sir Peter Gluckman
released a seminal paper on the better use of evidence in policy formation. He said this:
“policy formed without consideration of th e most relevant knowle dge available is far
less likely to serve the nation well”. He th en went on to say th is: “evidence-based
approaches must also lead to greater effici ency in the provision of public services. One
suspects that there are many Government-f unded programmes now in place that when
properly assessed would not meet objective tests of effectiveness; such evidence of non-
15566 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
performance would allow both the public and politicians to accept, and indeed require,
redirection of effort.”
The Children’s Commissioner, appointed by this Government, set up an expert
advisory group on solutions to child poverty in New Zealand. It reviewed both the
international and New Zealand literature. It  spoke to overseas experts and to local
experts. It talked to officials and to civi l society groups. It hear d submissions. It even
listened to members of Parliament.
In November 2013 the Health Committee released a comprehensive report on
improving child health outcomes from preconcep tion to 3 years of age. We listened to
officials. We read internat ional research and local rese arch from groups like the
Brainwave Trust and others. We came to the conclusion—we, the members of the select
committee: the National Party, the Labour Pa rty, New Zealand First, and the Greens—
that the Government needs “to put more  focus on and investment into the pre-
conception period to three years of age,”. We  said: “Such policy is not only backed by
science, equity, and ethics, but also makes sound economic sense.” I repeat that—sound
economic sense.
So why would this Government or any futu re Government not listen to the science,
the evidence, the ethics, and the economics of investing in our kids—investing in our
kids? You see, we have heard passionate sp eeches from the Government today about all
that it is doing for children. Nick Smith nods . So how is it, Dr Smith, that one of
Parliament’s select committees, the Expert  Advisory Group on Solutions to Child
Poverty, the Prime Minister’s own science adviser, and others are saying: “Listen to the
evidence.”? The evidence in New Zealand is  telling us that we  are not doing well by
children in New Zealand.
This Government says members on this side of the House have learnt nothing. I have
to say it is sad—it has learnt nothing. It learns nothing from evidence and nothing from
science. Well, I have to tell you that a Labour-led Government has and will. New
Zealanders have had enough of cheap words and flash slogans about the value and the
importance of our children. We hear the plat itudes. They are rolled out all the time—
lines like “Children are our greatest gift .”, “Children are our future.”, “We value
children.”, and “We are already doing so mu ch for children.” Well, the evidence shows
that that is hogwash.
We have some of the most appalling statistics relating to children in the OECD—the
OECD, countries we like to compare our selves with. Well, I am disgusted and
distressed when report after report shows that this country is failing its children. This is
a country that has so much. The Prime Minist er has said it is an egalitarian country.
When did he connect with Ne w Zealand? This country ha s not been an egalitarian
country in that way, probably, for 30 or 40 ye ars. We have seen slowly the destruction
of that egalitarian society, accelerated under this Government. We see statistics about
the high rate in this country of child accident s, of child abuse, of child poverty, of youth
suicide, and of failing educational achievement. You have got to ask yourself: where did
we go wrong?
The Prime Minister likes to say he wa s brought up in a St ate house, but this
Government, although it is building 1,000 extra,  does not tell you about the ones it has
knocked down, the ones it has closed up, and the thousands it has sold off. It does not
tell you how it treats State house tenants—as  worthless citizens. The Prime Minister
likes to say that he was br ought up on a widows benefit—plus the family benefit, and
maybe it could have even helped pay for th eir first own home. But “benefits” is now a
dirty word. Beneficiaries, especially thos e caring for children, are worthless in the
Government’s eyes. They are judged for their predicament.
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15567
Homeownership is now out of the reach of thousands of New Zealanders, and as for
giving a universal payment for children, that is now called an election bribe—the very
universal payment that helped Mr Key when he was a kid. Paula Bennett likes to crow
about how she got off the DPB and made good. She got a degree and she got it with a
training incentive allowance, but she got  rid of that allowance. Why has the
Government not stopped and asked itself a few questions? If the G overnment supports
families and if these policies supported the Prime Minister, Paula Bennett, and others
within the National Party, why is National denying those very policies for New Zealand
kids today? If those polices helped t hose members as children, why are they not
appropriate to help children today?
You see, it is all about priori ties. The reality is that the priorities have changed in
New Zealand, and children are no longer as impor tant to this Government as they were
in the past. Instead of seeing the future of our country in healthy, well-educated,
motivated children and families, this Government does not believe they are a priority. It
is now dog-eat-dog. Top dogs get the top dollars and the rest get the leftovers. It has to
change. It is going to take a Government with courage, with commitment, and with
priority.
I can assure New Zealanders that Labour members are totally committed to turning
round the position of children in New Zeala nd. Yesterday we announced Best Start,
based on evidence, research, and what Ne w Zealanders say needs to happen for
children. Why will that Government not open its ears and its eyes and for once look and
see what is happening to our kids and, instead of opposing everything, support it?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: What a fantastic speech
today, with the Prime Minister’s statement leading off the start of this parliamentary
year, 2014, which is going to be a fantas tic year for the Government and for the
National Party—a statement that, of course , those opposite do not believe. They do not
buy into it. They hate the fact that the economy is really starting to move—3.5 percent
from September to September last year. Is that not fantastic economic growth, when we
think about what is happening in the Cant erbury rebuild, helping those people get back
on their feet, and when we think about the big plans that we have for infrastructure in
this country? It is a fantastic Prime Minister’s statement.
We need to also acknowledge Bill English and the way that he steered this economy
forward over the last few years. We are all going to reap the bene fits of that going
forward. It was interesting that David Cun liffe, in his—whatever it was—state of
something speech, came out and suddenly magi cally said: “Oh, we’re not going to take
the GST off fruit and vegetables. We’re not  going to do something else on tax-free
status and that’s magically just generated $1.5 billion.” That is not at all budgeted in the
Government books. So therefore he just felt that he could come out with a delusional
policy and announce all of this stuff, which, ac tually, some have said is to encourage
those on incomes up to a leve l of $150,000 to have more babies Some have labelled it
middle-class welfare, and that is the way it wi ll be portrayed out there in the electorate.
We have a Labour Party that is old and tired.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How ignorant. What an ignorant member.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Annette has not got any new, fresh thinking. She has not got
any new ideas. For Mr Cunliffe to come into the House today and actually start
criticising primary industries, he is actually not in touch with what  is happening in our
rural communities. He does not feel a part of what is happening with the productive
sector of the economy, because for that $1.5 bi llion to be spent, it has to come from
somewhere. It has to come from the productiv e sector of this economy, and that is the
primary industries. It does not just drop out of the sky. It is not budgeted for. It is not
15568 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
factored in to our forecast going forward. Yet Labour just expects the primary industries
to pick it up.
Here we had Mr Cunliffe today, who is not in touch with rural communities. He
would not give a damn. He says that they ar e not adding value in the dairy industry. We
should be proud of the New Zealand dairy i ndustry and what it has achieved, exporting
to around 200 countries all around the world. What we have is  the fact that, of course,
Labour is opposed to anythi ng that is happening that is  productive in our primary
industries. It is against th e Trans-Pacific Partnership, which has the opportunity to
generate more income for our rural communities, more income, actually, for most of
New Zealand. It could potentially be $2 billion.
Labour is, of course, against other trade oppor tunities, as well. I cannot believe that.
We have also got the Primary Growth Part nership, which is a real showcase policy,
working well with those in the primary industries—17 projects  up and running,
supported by this Government, and $700 million invested. That is going to generate
billions and billions of dolla rs in research and development, and Labour is opposed to
that. Labour is opposed to research and deve lopment. This Govern ment is partnering
with primary industries to lift our growth pot ential, to put more products into different
markets. Labour is opposed to that. I cannot believe it.
It is also opposed to irrigation. This Government has invested $80 million and is
forecast to invest $400 million in total in dece nt water storage projects in our regional
economies. This, of course, is going to grow  our regional economies. It is also good for
the environment—

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Oh, yeah. OK. Poisoning water is great for the environment!

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: —because when water is stored  it takes the pressure off the
aquifers. You can maintain summer water fl ows, and, of course, that is good for the
aquatic and marine life. Of course, Moana Ma ckey chips in from the back seats over
there in Labour. It just goes to show that  Labour does not care a bout job creation. It
does not care about regional economies. [Interruption] I am sure that is Moana Mackey.
Labour does not even care about growing jobs in our regions. Here it is against research
and development. Here it is against irri gation. Here it is against opening up new
markets. We have just had a new market ope n up in Peru. Is Labour against that? Yes,
probably. We are working hard in other international markets as well. Russia and South
Korea are looking promising. We have got to  acknowledge the good work that Minister
Groser and Minister McCully do on the in ternational stage, supported by the Prime
Minister as well, to open up these international markets so that we can continue to grow
our primary industries, because you cannot ha ve policies rolled out, like the dopey one
that Labour announced just a couple of days ago, that cannot be supported by the
productive engine room of our economy.
We have $32 billion worth of exports at the moment. We have set a target of
doubling that to $64 billion. That is going to happen w ith the Primary Growth
Partnership. That is going to happen with mo re trade opportunities. That is going to
happen with water storage projects. Also  important is lifting the potential of M āori
agribusiness. That is where we are working closely with the regions like Northland. We
are looking at other opportunities over in the East Coast as well, where we need to
partner with iwi and other communities to lift their overall growing potential. If you
look at the potential in M āori agribusiness, there are a bout 1.5 million hectares owned
in multiple ownership of iwi, and about 300,000 hectares are under full production. If
we can lift the rest—the other 1.2 million hect ares—if we can lift the potential there,
that is worth an $8 billion prize in growing our exports. It is worth 3,500 jobs. That is
why we need to celebrate this Government and what we are trying to achieve in primary
industries.
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15569
Also in the Prime Minister’s speech he talked about the impor tance of biosecurity
and investing in our front line. We have got  100 new biosecurity officers that we have
rolled out in the last 14 m onths. That is hugely important . We have got 11 new X-ray
machines as well in our major airports, which is important and a real focus of mine. It is
my No. 1 priority. I need to acknowledge the work that the Ministry for Primary
Industries is doing right now in the Whan garei area, working closely with that
community, where we have had a fruit fly th at was detected in one of the traps up
there—a Queensland fruit fly. As a result of  that, we got 70 people on the ground there,
another 80 or 90 or so working as well, and a big response to ensure that we do more
trapping to hope that we do not  have any more fruit flies in that area. I want to
acknowledge the wonderful work that our bi osecurity people do and also acknowledge
the support of the Whangarei community in this response, and what it has been is a very
good response.
Also in the Prime Minister’s speech he talk ed about infrastructure. I cannot work out
whether Labour on the other si de of the House is  opposed to Transmission Gully or it
supports it.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: We don’t know.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: We do not know. We do not know. We might hear today.
What does Chris Hipkins think about Transm ission Gully? Does he support it or is he
against it?

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Support.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: He supports Transmission Gully. It is good that we now have
Labour on the record as supporting Transmissi on Gully. If we move up to the end of
Transmission Gully, where it comes into my electorate, the wonderf ul electorate of
Ōtaki, Labour is opposed to th e Kapiti Expressway. A thousa nd jobs will be created by
the Kapiti Expressway, and Labour is opposed to it. The biggest Government
investment in the Kapiti district, and Labour  does not give a damn. It does not give a
damn about my constituents sitting in a traffic jam getting into the capital city of New
Zealand. It does not give a damn  about freight getting through to the port here, or about
people getting to their hospita l appointments on time. It doe s not give a damn about the
Kapiti Expressway. It does not give a damn a bout infrastructure and investing in that in
the community. Of course, how do you grow  the productive engine room of the
economy? You make investments in roads.  You make investments in ultra-fast
broadband—200,000 people are going to benefit from the roll-out of ultra-fast
broadband—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: When?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: —in rural communities, and that is happening as we speak.
Annette King says “When?”, yet when she occasionally comes up in her van and sees
the people of Levin, she does not acknowledge the fact that ultra- fast broadband is
going to connect us not only domestically but internationally. This is a fantastic Prime
Minister’s statement, and it should be endorse d by every political party in this House.
Let us roll on to the 2014 election.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: If we needed a clear statement of the lack
of enthusiasm and lack of ideas that permeat e this National Government, we just had it.
We just had it from that member, Nathan Guy, who talked about the research and
development tax credit. Well, I have a que stion for him. Who cut the research and
development tax credit? Who was it that re moved the financial support for firms to
invest in research and development? Oh, that would be the current National
Government.
Of course, Nathan Guy argued that by pr oviding $60 a week for families who have
newborn children, we are going to be encour aging people to have a whole lot more
15570 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
babies. It is like saying that because New Zealand superannuation is universal, more
people are going to get old. No, that simply does not compute. It simply does not
compute. Is the Government arguing for m eans testing New Zealand superannuation? If
it has a problem with providing universal s upport to New Zealande rs, is it going to
means test New Zealand superannuation? Because  that is the logical extension of what
it has been arguing. Nathan Guy talked a bout Transmission Gully. After 5 years in
Government, not one sod has been turned for Transmission Gully, but I will tell you
what—there will be a sod turned in Ōtaki at the next general election. There will be a
sod turned in Ōtaki at the next general election—you can mark my words—because
Nathan Guy’s term in this Parliament will be coming to an end.
I want to talk about the fantastic announcem ents in the education area that David
Cunliffe made in his speech yesterday. We  will be extending free early childhood
education for 3 and 4-year-old s to 25 hours per week. That is something that I know
parents all around the country are going to be looking forward to and will welcome. We
have said that simply extending access is not  enough, however. We have also said that
we want to increase the quality of early childhood education in New Zealand and that
means that we will reinstate the commitment to having a fully qualified and registered
teaching profession in early childhood education. That is something that this
Government has moved away from.
It is interesting that Government member s are willing to talk about quality teaching
in schools, which is somethi ng that I support, but they ar e not willing to talk about
quality teaching in early childh ood education. In fact, they do not see that as a priority.
Giving kids the best possible start with their education—and that means investing in
quality early childhood educati on—is one of the most progre ssive things we can do for
the education system. That is why I am absolutely proud that Labour’s commitment to
increasing the number of hours that child ren can access is being accompanied by an
absolute commitment to increasing quality by  funding fully qualified teachers in early
childhood centres.
We also have to recognise that there are some parts of the country where the funding
model has been one of the contributing factors to a lack of provision, because the
current model that we have has seen most of  the growth in early childhood education in
the last decade or so come from the for-profit early childhood sector, and that has meant
that in many communities—or in a small nu mber of communities but vitally important
areas—there is underprovision, because the for-profits do not see a profit-making
opportunity in it. We actually have to get seri ous about that and that means that we will
put money in. We are unashamedly saying th at the Labour Government will put money
into building new centres where there is underprovision, because underprovision is—
particularly in many poor communities—one of  the contributing fact ors to those kids
not getting access to early childhood education.  That is the third leg of the stool of
Labour’s early childhood policy that David Cunliffe announced yesterday and I am
really, really proud to stand behind that.
It is a pretty clear contrast to the things that John  Key has been talking about—John
Key’s six-page apology for Heki a Parata, which he made last week. This, of course, is
the same Minister of Education who brought us school closures in Christchurch; who
thought that increasing the quality of education was going to rest on having bigger class
sizes; who brought us Novopay—if they are talking about increasing the pay for
teachers, there are still teachers around the country who are waiting to be paid at all as a
result of that botch-up—who brought us ch arter schools that do not have to have
qualified and registered teachers; who brought us national standards, which, of course,
have been proven to be neither national nor  standard; and who is now saying that the
Government wants to focus on the quality of teaching.
28 Jan 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15571
Well, I thought that was a ve ry interesting argument, be cause I think that quality
teaching is vitally important, but I do wa nt to pick up the comment by Graeme Aitken,
the Dean of Education at the University of  Auckland, who said in an opinion column
that there is an “Everest of research th at shows that socio-economic status is the
strongest predictor of achievement.” When the Government talks about quality teaching
being the strongest predictor of achievement, it is not actually corre ct. Quality teaching
is the strongest in-school pr edictor of student achievement; there is no argument about
that. But it is simply wrong for that Government to bury its head in the sand and claim
that all of the things that happen outside th e school do not have an impact on kids when
they get through the gate. As Graeme Aitk en has argued, the changes that the
Government announced last week will have “limited impact if they are not accompanied
by bold initiatives to address social inequa lity and poverty.” That is exactly what the
Labour Party has done this week with our Be st Start programme that David Cunliffe
announced yesterday.
I also want to quote—because I think this is actually really important when
considering the package that John Key announced around teaching last week—Graeme
Aitken on paying good teachers more. How is this Government going to decide what a
good teacher is? If it is going to decide it based on national standards and the National
Certificate of Educational Achievement, then  it is setting our e ducation system up for
failure. As Graeme Aitken has argued here: “Top teaching is not about cramming for
results”—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: What about the member’s own thoughts?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: —“on limited measures of learning. It is about leaving students
with greater enjoyment of reading, writing and mathematics and feeling confident about
new learning in these areas. It is also about opening students’ minds to the rich
curriculum offered in the arts, sciences, languages, technology, health and physical
education and the social sciences.”
I say to Gerry Brownlee that I agree with him. My thoughts are very, very similar to
his. I think he is absolutely right when he says that we cannot simply narrow the
definition of success in our e ducation system into cramming kids to pass a couple of
tests in a few areas. We actually have to give them a broad, we ll-rounded education.
That includes subjects lik e woodwork. Some kids do quite well in woodwork—
probably not the ones who had their educa tional opportunities completely hamstrung by
having the misfortune to have Gerry Brow nlee as their woodwork teacher, but many
kids do quite well in woodwork and they do fi nd that a bridge to other opportunities in
education. Kids learn quite well  in context, and I actually think, if we ar e talking about
numeracy, that kids doing woodwork quite often find woodwork a very good context in
which to learn better numeracy skills. They have to learn skills around measurement and
around all sorts of things; it is a good context.
But this Government does not s eem to think that is importa nt. It thinks that instead
you should be cramming kids full of literacy  and numeracy alone without the rich
context that comes from a broad curriculum, which is what I think we should be focused
on in our schools, and that is certainly—

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Where’s the science?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: “What about science?” I hear Moana Mackey saying. Science, of
course, is a vitally important part of th e curriculum as well. There are no national
standards in science. It is not a priority for this Government. Well, I think—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: All that stuff from Nathan Guy.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: After all that stuff from Nathan  Guy about science, it is a shame
that National does not seem to think that  science is important in schools. I think
employing a Chief Science Advisor to the Pr ime Minister was a very, very good idea. I
15572 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 28 Jan 2014
think that listening to him would be an ev en better idea, and th at is certainly not
something we are seeing from this Government.
Instead, of course, we have John Key and hi s dance of the desperate and dateless. It
is like political speed-dating over there on the National benches. We have got Colin
Craig, John Banks, and Peter Dunne. Peter Dunne is now restored to be a Minister of
the Crown. I am really interested to  know from John Key and from the National
Government who leaked the Kitteridge report.  Who leaked the Kitteridge report? If it is
happy to have Peter Dunne, the prime suspect fo r leaking the Kitteridge report, back in
the Government, it must think that some body else did it. How could John Key sack
Peter Dunne last year for leaking a Gove rnment document and then turn round and
reinstate him without actually establishing, if it was not Peter Dunne, who it was?

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Who done it?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Of course—who done it? But we know that this is nothing to do
with principle. This is everything to do w ith the desperate clinging to power by this
National Government, which is out of ideas and which is out of energy. It is time, and in
the coming election it will be replaced. It  will be replaced and there will be a
Government with a commitment to ensuring that all New Zealanders share in the
economic recovery that is taking place—all Ne w Zealanders get their fair share of that.
That is not going to happen under this Gove rnment, which is committed to the trickle-
up theory that sees all of the wealth con centrated in fewer and fewer New Zealanders,
while those in the middle get squeezed, and t hose on the lowest incomes get absolutely
clobbered.
The days of those policies are coming to an  end. We have to bring in fairness. We
have to restore the balance. We have to restore a fair and just society in which every
New Zealander is rewarded appr opriately for their efforts, every child in this country
gets the best possible start in  life, every school is a great school, and every teacher is a
great teacher. This is not about picking winners; it is a bout giving every body their fair
opportunities in life.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I move, That this debate be
now adjourned.
Motion agreed to.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: There is about a minute or so
before the dinner break. I seek the leave of  the House for the House to lift now and
resume at 7.30.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is
there any objection? There is no objection.
Sitting suspended from 5.59 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I move, That the Subantarctic
Islands Marine Reserves Bill be now read a second time . We have just come from
debating the Prime Minister’s statement, in which he outlined the ambition of his
Government to create a record number of mari ne reserves this year, and it is entirely
appropriate that the House now works on pr ogressing three very substantive marine
reserves, covering 430,000 hectares in the subantarctic area.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Smaller than the oil blocks.
28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15573

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I hear interjections from the Green Party. There is sort of
the view that the bigger gains that are ma de for conservation and the environment are
made by the political left. Let me put Mr Gareth Hughes correct. The Marine Reserves
Act, which was a world leader, was passed in 1971 by a National Government. The very
first marine reserve created in New Zeala nd was in 1976: the Leigh reserve north of
Auckland. Of the 34 marine reserves that ha ve been created in New Zealand, the vast
bulk of them have been created by National administrations, and we are proud of that. I
would also point out that in  the term of this Governme nt we passed very important
legislation to put in place proper environmental regulati on of our exclusive economic
zone. So this Government—

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: It’s not proper.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Well, I hear Moana Mackey from the opposite side interject
and say that she questions that legislation. I remind that member that she and the Greens
sat in this Parliament for 9 years, allowed deep-sea drilling, and did not raise a finger—

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: None of it happened under a Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Yes, it did. There was deep-s ea drilling for 9 years during
Labour’s Government, with no environmenta l regulation, and there was not a squeak
from the Green Party during that period, wh ich really does expose the double standards
that we witness in some of the arguments about the marine space. But I am absolutely
pleased that this bill recei ves the very wide support of Parliament, and I want to
acknowledge the good work that the Local Government and Environment Committee,
under Nicky Wagner’s very able leadership, has made to this bill.
I would remind the House that  the Subantarctic Islands  do have World Heritage
status. It is actually a status that I was involved in establishing in the 1990s, when I was
also the Minister of Conservation. What this  Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill
does is enable—through the collaborative pr ocess that was set up back in 2008, which
provided a report to Minister s in 2010—us to proceed with the agreement of the key
stakeholders that participated in that forum on the creation of these new marine reserves
in the Antipodes Islands, the Bounty Islands, and Campbell Island.
This Government does believe that the be st way forward with issues like marine
conservation is not the very l ong, the very protracted, and the very divisive sorts of
arguments that we have seen in places like Akaroa, but by actually getting stakeholders
working together in the collaborative way th at has delivered five proposed marine
reserves on the West Coast and these three ma rine reserves here. Another issue for the
Government to work through this year is  the proposals for marine protection in
Kaikōura that have come from the Te Korowa i o Te Tai o Marokura process. So I do
want to acknowledge the strength of that collaborative process, which has brought about
these proposals.
There have been amendments proposed by the select committee in respect of the
review of the reserv e around the Campbell Island area. I think the changes that have
been recommended by the select committee ma ke good sense. There has been the issue
of the timing—whether it should be 5 years be fore the review of the area in Campbell
Island takes place. That has been shortened by the select committee to 3 years. Given
the fact that 18 months have passed in between, that makes good sense, and the
Government will be supporting those ch anges. I would also acknowledge the
improvements that have been made to the bill on some of the details.
I know that with every environmental ini tiative that this G overnment makes—or,
frankly, that the previous Government made—t he Green Party always says that it is
never enough. There is nothing new about that. I am going to have a heart attack the day
the Green Party ever gets up and says: “Yes , that’s good and that ’s enough and we’re
satisfied.” It has not happened once—it has not happened once—with any initiative
15574 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 28 Jan 2014
made by a Labour or a National Government in  the 16-odd years that the Green Party
has been part of this Parliament.
The last point that I want to make on this bi ll is to just note the very special ecology
of the three Subantarctic  Islands areas that we are looking to protect here. It  is true that
the ocean environment is the new frontier for conservation. Seventy percent of the
species that are endemic to New Zealand—70 percent—are not actually on land, where
all the terrestrial concentration has been. They are actually out there in the marine
environment, and that is why this Governme nt is giving a particular focus to marine
conservation. It is my intention, which I wa nt to give the House notice of, to table a
Supplementary Order Paper duri ng the Committee stage just to note that we want to
bring the reserve in as quickly as possible afte r the passage of the bill. Other than that I
think it is in good shape, and I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: We will be supporting this  bill, the Subantarctic
Islands Marine Reserves Bill. We welcome the creation of three new marine reserves:
Moutere Mahue, or the Antipodes Island Mari ne Reserve; Mouter e Hauriri, or the
Bounty Islands Marine Reserve; and Mout ere Ihupuku, or the Campbell Island Marine
Reserve. As the Minister of Conservation said, these are indeed incredibly unique
ecosystems, World Heritage sites, and they de serve the protection that  this bill will be
affording them. It is important, coming out of the select committee, to note that the
majority of submitters to the Local Gove rnment and Environment Committee did want
the extension of those marine reserves. I do not think I have seen the creation of a
marine reserve where people have not wanted to see it extended. There are always good
reasons and we need to be mindful of those.
We have a particularly successful marine reserve at Puoawa up off the East Coast,
where over time that marine reserve was act ually extended over the reef at Whangar ā
because of the unique ecosystem there and, in fact, in the meantime the locals and the
local fishermen—and anyone who worked in that area, actually—abided by an
unofficial marine reserve because they coul d see the sense of that. I can tell you, the
best fishing on the East Coast is on the borde rs of the marine reserve. Anyone who says
that no one will know where those borders ar e just needs to look at where the fishing
boats are, and that will tell you.
I remember going with the Hon Chris Ca rter, when he was the Minister of
Conservation, to have a look at the success of that marine reserve. It had been highly
controversial. There is this idea of lock ing up the ocean, which I always found slightly
odd, given that fish are going to freely move in  and out of the marine reserve. But we
have had some serious issues with crayfi sh stocks on the East Coast and with the
overfishing of that particular species. There was a PhD student there and she was doing
her PhD on this particular marine reserve. It had been in place for only 4 years. Outside
the marine reserve she was finding about half a kilogram of legal-sized crayfish per pot,
and inside the marine reserve it was 30 kil ograms of legal-sized cray per pot. I do not
know how the crayfish knew to stay within the marine reserve—I am not quite sure
what kinds of communications were going on th ere—but we also saw the restoration of
stocks that we had not seen on the East Coast in a while, in numbers that were
significant. So, hopefully, I do not think you ne ed to convince anyone in this House of
the benefits of marine rese rves, and for our part we are very pleased to see this
extension and we would like to see further extensions of marine reserves.
Can I also say how nice it is to have a pi ece of legislation at the Local Government
and Environment Committee that is not di abolically awful and damaging for the
environment. So on the one hand the Government giveth and on the other hand it taketh
away massively. It is a balance, I guess, which seems to be a phrase that comes up
constantly in environmental law and environmen tal protections. But it was nice to have
28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15575
a really positive piece of le gislation, notwithstanding that some people wanted it to go
further, and to be able to look at the photos and the images and learn more about a part
of the world that most of us will never go to but is incredibly important to the entire
marine ecosystem. So that is the good stuff.
I cannot let the Minister’s comments go without commenting on the protection of
Māui’s dolphins, because although I am quite happy to acknowledge that  this is a bill
that is going to strengthen marine protecti on and the marine environment, on the other
hand we saw in September last year th e Government’s decision to oppose further
protection measures for M āui’s and Hector’s dolphins, so me of the most endangered
mammals on our planet. New Zealand was one of just two countries to vote against new
protections for these dolphins  at the International Union for Conservation of Nature
conference in Korea.
For New Zealand to stand up on an in ternational stage and oppose a motion to
protect one of the most enda ngered dolphin species in the wo rld kind of runs up against
all the really good stuff the Hon Dr Nick Smith was saying right now about marine
conservation, protecting marine ecosystems,  and protecting the marine environments.
The actions, as the Minister will be aware,  did cause environmen tal concern, and they
do not make economic sense. Our future is not in unsustainable fishing practices at all.
Just as we have this debate between the Government side of the House and the
Opposition side of the House about our “cl ean, green” branding generally across our
environment and climate change issues, we see that same branding being incredibly
important to our fishing industry. On this side of the House we believe that New
Zealand really does have an opportunity to be a truly su stainable fishery, and the
protection of M āui’s and Hector’s dolphins  absolutely has to be at the top of that. So,
again, Minister, here we are debating a very good piece of legislation where—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: We’re extending the protection for Māui’s.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Yes, Minister, but we voted against proper protections on an
international stage—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: No, we didn’t.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Yes, we did. The protections have not gone as far as every
single expert who is working in the area  of the conservation of Hector’s and M āui’s
dolphins has told us we need to do if we do not want to see a native species die out and
become extinct on our watch—die out and beco me extinct on our watch. And so I think
that it is highly unfortunate that the Government cannot extend this wonderful ethos that
we heard from the Hon Dr Nick Smith about marine protection right across all areas of
policy and not just have it in one area—cyni cally perhaps—because it is election year.
Maybe that is cynical but you get that way in this place.
I want to come back to another issue as well that I think flie s against the very good
ethos we have heard here about the protec tion of marine environments, and that is
actually the protection of our other waterways, which feed into our marine environment,
all of which is part of one great big ecosystem. It does worry me sometimes when I hear
National Government Ministers just say that we should not have any kind of water from
rivers flowing out into the ocean, because it is  a waste; we should put it all in a dam. I
mean, water storage is a fine idea—

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: That’s outrageous.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Go back and have a look at what the Minister said. It is a great
idea, but having water go out to the ocean is not a waste. It is actually a really important
part of an ecosystem. At the moment we have a very important  process going on to
decide about a water storage system in the Hawke’s Bay that would turn the Tukituki
River catchment toxic. It will turn the Tukitu ki toxic. That is th e concern of the many
environmental groups and experts who have appeared before a truncated board of
15576 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 28 Jan 2014
inquiry process that has been geared agai nst community organisations. The Department
of Conservation, for some reason—and maybe the Hon Nick Smith can enlighten us as
to what that reason was—saw fit to produce a large submission on the Dunedin City
Council discharging more stormwater but di d not see fit to provide a submission on
whether or not the Ruataniwha Dam scheme would turn the Tukituki River catchment
toxic. I am not sure why that is, the Hon Dr Nick Smith. Maybe you might have more of
an idea about that than me. So the burden has fallen—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: The department decided that.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Oh, the department had decided that! No one believes that for
a second. So what we have is that the burden has fallen to community groups, to
individuals, to local iwi, and to NGOs to pick up where the Government has slacked off
and has not done its job in protecting the c onservation of our waterways. So we have
got a truncated process. We have NGOs, co mmunity organisations, individuals, and iwi
who have not been properly consulted, who were messed around before Christmas,
given days in the lead-up to Christmas to change the times that they were doing their
submissions and were given mere days for rebuttal.
We have a process that is not protecting our waterways a nd that the public can have
no confidence in. There is no doubt that a number of these schemes are going to be
controversial. That is why th e process is so important. Th at is why the Government’s
role is to ensure that the best analysis is done of water quality issues and that any issue
that goes through this board  of inquiry and the Enviro nmental Protection Authority
process is done to the highest standard a nd highest transparency, and is not just a
rubber-stamping exercise that is  going to turn th e Tukituki catchment  toxic. That is
what it is going to do. That is what the experts are telling us it is going to do. We should
be having a far greater look in that scheme at the single nutrient management system
that is being proposed.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Is Labour opposed to the scheme?

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: We are opposed to an absolu tely dodgy process that is not
going to ensure that the environment is protected, Dr Smith.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Ah! She’s not saying.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: No, I am waiting to see what the board of inquiry comes out
with, and—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Oh, so are we.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Well, I think we know. I think we  know, but I am prepared to
give the process its shot. But from everyt hing I have heard from people on the ground,
Dr Smith, we know what the result is going to  be. You know what the result is going to
be. That is why you refused to put anyone wi th a water science speciality on to the
board of inquiry—because they might actually know what they are talking about.
I want to finish up by just referring to Dr Nick Smith’s comments about the exclusive
economic zone legislation. Here  is another example where Na tional thinks that it can
put something incredibly weak in place and use it as an excuse for not doing something
that would actually protect the exclusive economic zone. There were eight deep-sea
wells drilled before the exclusive economic zone legislation came into place. When we
went and had a look at them, they were under National Governments in the 1990s and in
the 1980s. [Interruption] Yes, they were, in the exclus ive economic zone. So when the
bill first came to the House, we thought: “ OK, maybe the better-than-nothing argument
actually is a good one.” But when we read through it, the bill was such a dog and such a
developers’ charter that we could not give  the National Governme nt the excuse of
saying that this had complete and total support in Parliament, because it was not
adequate. It is so much weaker than the Re source Management Act. So we have drawn
a line in the ocean, a line that is jurisdicti onal only, and said that on this side we are
28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15577
going to have proper environmen tal protections, and on that side we are going to have
pretty much no environmental protections, no ri ght for the public to have their say, no
right for the public to go out and protest—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! The time has concluded.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Oh, but I was just really getting going.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to hear that. You have now finished.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Thank you for giving me the
opportunity to speak in support of the second reading of the Subantarctic Islands Marine
Reserves Bill. I was interested in the comments of the previous speaker, Moana
Mackey, that Labour may be opposing the Ruat aniwha project ther e in the Tukituki.
That is something I have not seen as a pub lic statement by the leader, but Hawke’s Bay
listeners tonight will be interested in that information. I, of course, am pleased that the
Minister of Conservation, Nick Smith, is br inging forward the legislation that we have
got here before us. He did that  before Christmas, and we ha ve looked at it in the Local
Government and Environment Committee.
It was 3 years ago today, in fa ct, that I, as Minister of Fisheries, and Kate Wilkinson,
the then Minister of Conservation, announced  that these three huge  marine reserves,
totalling over 435,000 hectares, were to be esta blished in the Subantarctic Islands. We
were very proud of that at that time. A considerable am ount of work has been done
since because there has been a high level of public engagement, which is usually the
case when the National Government is doing environmental law. Then action occurs.
There will be marine reserves after us.
It is true that Labour and the Greens do lik e to consult more. They do; they go round
and round and round again. They do not reach a conclusion. They do not make a
decision. People are consulted with thoroughl y. They do indeed run a very robust
consultation process. We, on the other hand, pr efer to have consu ltation and get better
ideas from the community than we have at the current time, once we have put
something on paper. Then we make a decision,  and in this case, of course, we have.
There will be marine reserves. We will not be going out for years and years of more
cyclical conversations, love-ins, and hugs, which the Green  Party and the Labour Party
seem to need. We have made a decision here, and these marine reserv es will be put in
place.
So we will see a marine reserve cover the entire territorial sea out to 12 nautical
miles, surrounding the Antipodes Island, with two further marine reserves around the
Bounty Islands and Campbell Island. At the ti me we made the original decision, it was
covering about 58 percent and 39 percent of those islands’ territorial seas, respectively.
There are prohibitions today in seining. Th ey will be introduced in the remaining
territorial sea. Of course, these islands as a land mass boast World Heritage status, in
recognition of their internati onal conservation importance;  what we are essentially
doing is extending this to the sea mass. I reme mber Kate Wilkinson at the time saying
that some of the most biologically diverse marine communities in the world are found
here, and recent research shows that their di versity compares to locations such as the
Galapagos Islands. So it is no wonder that we have good cross-party support for this
legislation. I just thank the Minister Nick Sm ith for making sure that it is cemented in
and for, essentially, carrying the ball, I gue ss, and doing the work to get this over the
line and drive it through Parliament, as is hi s habit. So as a pr evious Minister of
Fisheries involved in this decision some y ears ago, I would like to  thank the Minister
Nick Smith for taking this on and making sure that it happens.
I do want to thank the Subantarctic Islands  Marine Protection Planning Forum, at
that time chaired by Buddle Findlay part ner Paul Beverley, which conducted a
tremendous amount of work consulting on and assessing the marine protection options.
15578 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 28 Jan 2014
When complete, the new marine protected areas will boost the area of New Zealand’s
territorial sea that is prot ected to over 10 percent, which is a wonderful record. I do
know that Minister Nick Smith is very passi onate about marine reserves. Before I was a
member of Parliament, I reca ll him bringing in the mari ne reserve out of the Poor
Knights Islands, off the Northland coast, whic h was quite controversial at that time. I
recall that the Green Party and the Labour Party had talked a lot about that too for many,
many years, and consulted and talked, and consulted and talked some more. They do
like to talk. They do like to consult. We like to make decisions. Here is something again
that is concrete and not just empty promis es, hot air, and love-ins. Thank you, Minister
Nick Smith. I look forward to supporting this bill as it goes through the Committee
stage and the third reading.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: The Labour Party is proud to support
this Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves  Bill. We want to support this because,
actually, Labour started the process to bring ab out these marine reserves. It is not about
“love-ins” or anything like that, as Mr Heatley seems to suggest. We started this in 2006
and 2007. As he said, the bill has sat there and languished for some time since he was
Minister of Fisheries, and now he is no longer fisheries Minister and it still goes on.
Yet, here we are, at the second reading.
It is, however, good that we are able to progress this bill this evening. It is something
that I believe all New Zealanders will be very pleased to see. It will extend that
protection out much further. Right now the terrestrial elements of those islands are
under protection but not actually the sea around them. This w ill enable this pristine and
very biologically diverse and biologically precious area to be protected properly and
fully.
The concept of marine reserves is somethi ng that the Labour Party is, in general,
supporting. It is Labour Party policy to extend the protections of ma rine reserves to
about 30 percent of the area under New Zeala nd’s jurisdiction by the year 2020. That is
something that we want to move on. It is something that I would encourage the National
Party to actually put in its manifesto as well, because we have made a good start in
being bipartisan on this partic ular issue and it would actually  be rather good for it to be
taken further along.
These islands, as I have said and as ev erybody knows and as has been said before,
have extraordinary biological significance. But as a result of that they also have some
economic significance in the form of tourism.  We are seeing more boats going down to
these areas so that people ar e able to take a l ook for themselves and actually experience
the diversity that is there too. So although th ere has been some talk about the economic
cost, there is also a huge economic benefit. Th at will also contribu te to New Zealand’s
standing internationally in te rms of our ability to have is lands of such significance
available.
As I said, the Labour Party is very proud and pleased to be able to support this bill. It
also adjusts or rebalances some of the policies by this Government, which have come up
before international fora anyway, that have  been less significant and certainly more
embarrassing to our country. I am talking of the debacle over the Ross Sea and trying to
get an agreement that was actually—we coul d have had an agreement with the United
States over the Ross Sea, but we lost that opportunity. We lost the opportunity to protect
that area, for the sake of around a $20 milli on fishing industry, I think, which would not
have been closed out completely but certa inly would have been affected. When we
balance that up against the hundreds of millions of dollars that we get in benefit as a
result of our reputation and al so as a gateway to the Antarctic that the United States is
using, I think that was an enormous missed opportunity to actually put some sort of
credentials down there as well.
28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15579
The other area, of course, that we have b een less illustrious on is the protection of
Māui’s dolphins and Hector’s dolphins. We we re one of two countries that actually
went against the international agreement to  protect these very precious mammals—the
most endangered species of dolphins in the world.
On a personal note, I remember some year s ago being out surfing off the west coast
off O’Neills Beach. I was paddling out there, and some of the surfers around me called
out “Shark! Shark!”, and swung their boards round and took a wave in to get away from
what they thought was a shark. I was a little more slow off the mark—unfortunately, I
am not as quick as some of those guys—but I had the opportunity of seeing two of these
enchanting dolphins swim around me, within 10 metres of me, and disappear. So being
slow off the mark in that particular case was to my advantage. I was actually able to see
these dolphins in the wild, up close. Those small round fins and the way that they were
able to move through the water certainly made  me feel not only very privileged to see
them but also pretty determined to make sure that these dolphins actually survive. If we
were ever to lose these dolphins as a re sult of the policies th at we are about to
implement and the fact that we are unable and unwilling to sign up to an international
protection for these dolphins, I think it would be an absolute travesty.
