I am very pleased to once again be here to provide support as a speaker from the
Labour Party to ensure that these islands in the south of  New Zealand do actually get
protection. They were awarded World Heritage status in 1998. The marine reserves and
the prohibitions on Danish purse seining, co mbined with the existing Fisheries Act
regulations and prohibitions on bottom trawling and dredging, will provide those marine
protected areas in the wide r area of the territorial sea of New Zealand and the
Subantarctic Islands with the sort of protection that they are going to need.
There will be some impact on commercial fisheries. I note that some of the ling
fisheries will be extended. From the regulatory impact statement that I have seen and
read, the way that these ling are taken has a very small bycatch. As a result of that, the
phasing out of that ove r the next 5 years will be welc omed, but obviously it will be up
for review at the end of that time. Of course, this legislation will also be up for review
within the course of 5 years.  That is a good initiative. I think it needs to be done
between 5 years and 7 years. That will ensure that our fisheries are well reviewed, and
ensure that the Subantarctic  Islands Marine Reserves Bill—which I am sure will go
through Parliament—is working in the way that  we would like it to, and ensure that the
protections are being afforded as we would like them to be.
It is certainly with pride that we are able to come together today with the
Government and, I believe, all parties in the Parliament to protect an area that will serve
New Zealand well in terms of its reputation. It will serve those marine ecosystems well
in terms of their unique fauna and flora that  are found in those S ubantarctic Islands,
which have been compared to the Galapagos  Islands, for example, and, as I say, have
been awarded World Heritage status. That wi ll also enable us to further develop the
tourism potential in those places, and ensure that there is some economic benefit that
comes back to us that can be put back into  ensuring that these islands are well and truly
protected. So it is with those few words that I would like to conclude my comments
today and to once again ensure that Labour w ill be supporting this bill in its entirety.
Thank you very much.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a
koutou. Kia ora. I would like to wish all th e members in the House and people listening
over the TV, the live stream, or the radio a very happy New Year, and I wish them all
the best for 2014. Of course we celebrate gr eat Kiwis doing great stuff, like Lorde.
Obviously, it is election year and we kicked  off the debate with the Prime Minister’s
statement. We saw a robust debate. I think all of us are going to pu t our values, visions,
15580 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 28 Jan 2014
and solutions for this country forward, and it is going to be an exciting year because
being an Opposition party, as the member Dr  Nick Smith points out often, the Greens
are opposed to things, but in election year  the Greens are going to be going out there
putting out our positive solutions and vision. I th ink we have got a great deal of that, so
I relish the opportunity this year to talk a bout the positive things, the things that make
our country good.
I echo the sentiment of Dr Russel Norman. Th is year we can make history. When it
comes to ocean protection and protection of our  beautiful Subantarctic Islands, this year
we can make history and take it seriously. I am glad we did finally hear from the Labour
Party that it started the pr ocess. Listening to the Hon Dr Nick Smith, you would think
he had come in dressed as Neptune himself with a bit of seaweed on his hair and his
trident, for all of his talk of being the champion of marine protection. I welcome the
Government taking marine protection seriously. I want to see more action. I want to see
more talk. I want to see more consultation. But here is the Minister making out like he is
the greenest thing since whatever the greenest thing was.
What we see is the year starting on marine  reserves. I think that is great for our
country. It is great for our environment. It is great for our economy. Kiwis love our
marine reserves. We were pioneering in 1971. I have got to somewhat point out the
irony to Dr Nick Smith that here he is co ming in as the champion of marine reserves
pointing out the National Party’s history. It is somewhat ironic that it has taken 40 years
to get to this point with thes e areas, but even more ironic that the legislation that he
refers to from 1971 has been bypassed. We actually need legislation of the Parliament to
see these marine reserves adopted. It is  not good enough. I think we can all agree on
that. Obviously, we saw two marine reserve bills languishing in select committees, the
second-oldest in our Parliament’s history.
I would like to reopen the invitation made to your pr edecessor Kate Wilkinson—I
have made it to you yourself—that the Gr een Party wants to work constructively
because it is high time we modernise our an tiquated yet pioneering for its time marine
reserve legislation. I mean that seriously. I wa nt to work with the Government, be it a
blue or a red one, because it is high time we actually addressed the fact that we cannot
make marine reserves in th e exclusive economic zone. The criteria for getting marine
reserves off the ground are incr edibly difficult, so let us work together. We need to
protect more of our waters. We do need to do more. It is great to be seeing marine
reserves around the Subantarctic Islands. I ha ve never been there my self. I really hope
to get there. I doubt very many New Zealanders will get to see this ve ry special part of
the country. Although the Minister is trumpe ting the size—it is s ubstantial at 430,000
hectares—that, of course, is considerably sm aller than just this year’s petroleum block
offer. Just 1 year of oil blocks, massively, is  larger than this. What did the Minister call
it? Trumpeting this particular ma rine reserve. So it is great to see it but let us put it in
context.
We need to do more. These marine reserv es take New Zeala nd’s percentage of
marine reserve protection from only 0.31 percen t to 0.41 percent. So less than half of 1
percent of New Zealand’s wate rs, the fourth-largest in the world, are protected.
Obviously, it is around 79 per cent for the territorial sea,  but when you look at the
exclusive economic zone, it is less than half of 1 percent. We want to work with the
Government to see more of our waters pr otected. When you look at all the academic
studies, we know there are si gnificant local economic bene fits. When you look at the
studies, you see there are significant fisherie s benefits and biodiversity benefits—win-
win-win for communities. The collaborative process has been good to help stimulate
some of those discussions. There have been some controversial ones in the past.
28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15581
The Minister also liked to point out that the Greens will never celebrate the
Government’s good decisions. That is just not right. It is not on. I think in the space of a
single week I was tweeting in support of the Akaroa mari ne reserve decision and the
decision to finally ban shark finning—in a single week. I would like to acknowledge the
Akaroa decision because there you really see the nexus of the environmental and
economic benefits. There are around 200 busines ses directly related to the environment
in Akaroa and in the harbour. The small marine reserve and the Tai āpure played a
significant economic role in that beautiful township. It is great that we are finally seeing
progress there. But we need to do more  than having 0.41 percent of our waters
protected.
What we would be pushing for is greater m odernisation of the le gislation, a greater
focus on working collaboratively with people. Again, it is somewhat ironic that former
Minister Heatley comes down to the House a nd bangs the table and talks about how the
Government, the National Party, is all abou t action, action, action. But we also heard in
this debate that these areas were gazetted as World Heritage areas in 1998 under a
National Government, which did not protect th em then. This Government has been in
power for 5 years and it has taken until this point, the election year, to finally get on and
do it under legislation. Maybe the action call is not as apt as the Minister made out.
What we would like to point out is that we support the Subantarctic Islands Marine
Reserves Bill. We would like to thank the submitters, the Local Government and
Environment Committee members, and the ch airperson, Nicky Wagner. We think that
the bill was improved in the select committ ee. The fact that the review for full
protection has been pushed forward is a good thing. But what we were urging, and you
can read it in our minority report, is the fact  that these are World Heritage listed areas.
They should be fully protected. I think it makes a mockery of protection to see only
percentages. It is 39 percent of Campbell Island and 58 percent of the Bounty Islands.
The rationale is the potential crab fishery in  the future. I challenge any member to say
who is going to be marketing crabs caught in  a World Heritage area and exporting them
around the world. I do not think that they wi ll find many consumers, particularly in
those premium markets that we should really be going on.
I welcome the focus for marine reserves. If  the Government wants to have an arms
race, a competition, when it comes to protect ing our waters, I welcome that because we
have got some really good policies when it comes to that area. When it comes to the
Māui’s dolphin, we have a protection plan that would stop the trawling that is
happening in the marine mammal sanctuary. We would end the mockery of our marine
protection laws, which see that in the bent hic protected areas fi shers cannot fish 100
metres above the seabed, yet a company can l iterally vacuum up the top 5 metres of the
seabed—a protection area that does not o ffer protection. We see an oil well in the
middle of a marine mammal sanctuary. We see the Government this year in the
petroleum Block Offer 2014 literally offer deep -sea oil permits that cross into a marine
mammal sanctuary around Akaroa. Good on the Christchurch City Council and Vicki
Buck, in particular, who made a submissi on to the Government opposing that, pointing
out the risks of deep-sea drilling.
What we would do is have sanctuaries that  actually provide sanc tuary and protected
areas that actually provide protection. We would set an ambitious target for marine
reserve protection around the country. We would update the antiquated Marine Reserves
Act. Again, the invitation goes out that we want to work with the Government to
modernise this old-fashioned legislation. A good green Government that comes in and
makes history could start by protecting the Kermadec Islands. Overnight, New Zealand
could go from less than half of 1 percent to 15 percent of our waters protected in marine
reserves by expanding the marine reserve ar ound the Kermadec Islands. For the cost of
15582 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 28 Jan 2014
only around $120,000 per annum of fishing we c ould send a message to the world that
New Zealand takes this seriously. We have an economy built on smart sustainability
that takes environmental issues like conser vation seriously. That is where our economy
is coming from and that is why I am pushi ng incredibly hard, after the Greens won the
shark-finning victory, to protect the Kermadec Islands. We want to work with all parties
to do that.
We would start the development of an in tegrated oceans policy, which has been
talked about for years and year s but we need action. So all in  all the Green Party stands
for protecting our waters and protecting th e economy, which depends on our beautiful
environment. As New Zealanders, we should say that this is something that should unite
us. I grew up in Gisborne , on the East Coast, where every summer we would go
camping at the same beach, Pouawa. That is where I learnt to surf, and it is where I
would go out with my dad and put out a cray  pot. I think every New Zealander has got
that story.
We heard of David Sheare r’s story about seeing M āui’s dolphins live in the marine
environment when he was out surfing. I think it is an incredible tale, and it is a tale our
kids and our grandkids unfor tunately may miss out on. But it is not too late; we can
protect our M āui’s dolphins. We can see more of our waters protected. We can see a
thriving fishing industry built on sustainability. We can pr otect our waters from the
other threats facing them, like deep-sea dril ling and like vacuuming up the seabed with
some of the incredibly crazy marine mi ning proposals. A Government that takes it
seriously is a green Government. That is  why I think you will see that a good green
Government will make history protecting our waters, protecting our environment,
protecting our economy, and protecting the things we love.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Just, perhaps, a few facts about National’s
record. In the 5 years of the National Government, we have announced nine new marine
reserves, which will significantly increase biodiversity protection in New Zealand
waters. So that is nine new marine reserves.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Nine—and that is nine new mari ne reserves over a period of 5
years in Government, so I think that is a pretty good record. New Zealand currently has
34 type 1 marine reserve areas and 14 type 2 marine reserv e areas or other management
tools. That covers just over 7 percent and just over 1 percent of the territorial sea,
respectively. National has got a pretty good record in this area. Approximately 9.5
percent of New Zealand’s territo rial sea will be protected by marine reserves once the
three new Subantarctic Islands marine rese rves are gazetted, a nd those are the three
marine reserves that are contained in this bill, the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves
Bill.
Just, perhaps, a reference to  the previous speaker, Ga reth Hughes, and the Green
Party minority report that it put into this bill, where it talked about  0.41 per cent being
covered by marine reserves. This refers to marine reserves as a percentage of New
Zealand’s economic zone, not of the territoria l sea, so I stand by th e percentage of 9.5
percent of New Zealand’s territorial sea be ing covered by marine reserve status once
this bill is enacted. That member is also abso lutely correct in that National has a proud
history of marine protection. In 1971 we pa ssed the original Marine Reserves Act and
established the first marine reserve, and th at was at Leigh in 1975. Incidentally, Leigh
was one of the very first no-take reserves in the world. So I stand by National’s proud
record and I stand by the record of the Hon Nick Smith in his sponsorship of this bill.
The proposal for the marine reserves is the result of a pretty extensive and
collaborative stakeholder forum, with a lot of  input from iwi, indus try representatives,
scientific conservation groups, and also the wider public. That kind of consultation, and
28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15583
collaborative consultation, is one of the hallmarks of this  National Government. It has
been undertaken in a number of other forums and it is proving to be  very successful, as
indeed it is with this marine protection legislation.
Just for a little bit of background, although the three isla nd groups contained in the
bill have protected land area status, the terr itorial waters around them are not currently
protected in marine protected status. They do not have that status as it applies to the
land. So the proposal recognises great opportunitie s for tourism, for scientific research,
and, of course, for fishing in a responsible  and sustainable way. Although I appreciate
the words of the Green member of Parliament , with him saying that in their view there
should be no fishery take in these marine pr otected areas, I have a different view, as
does the Minister of Conservati on. That is why there will be protection in this bill for
the ling fishery and also a possible exploration for a crab fishery.
This is a thoughtful bill. It was considered well by the Local Government and
Environment Committee. I do commend it to the House.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Can I just extend my greetings to all members
of this House at the beginning of 2014, and also to all those out  there who may be
listening to this broadcast. It is great to start the parliamentary year at the end of January
with already so much on the agenda.
The Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bi ll is a very interesting bill. I have had
the great pleasure in the last  couple of weeks to be down in what you would say is as
close as you can possibly get, on mainland Ne w Zealand, to this area. I visited Stewart
Island, Fiordland, and Queenstown. When you go down there and you see what has
been done in terms of the—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: You’re not going to stand in Clutha-Southland, are you?

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: No, no, I am not going to stand in Southland, no. When
going down into your area, Mr Deputy Speaker , into Eric Roy country, and seeing what
is being done on the likes of Stewart Island, with Ulva Island and the marine reserve

The Local Government and Environment Com mittee was very privileged last year to

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: —others say it is the fourth-l argest, and others say it is

items.text: No, no, I am sorry, Minister. No, no, we cannot let you get

New Zealand First does continue to have c oncerns about the leve l of funding to the

28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15585
When I was tramping the Routeburn Track la st week, we were th e only Kiwis in the

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I rise to talk to the Subantarctic
Islands Marine Reserves Bill at its second r eading. As others have noted, this is a bill

other members of the Local Government and Environment Committee, I regret that we
were not able to go there in person and sample  their delights, because this is a unique
part of the world. Perhaps because it is so remote and it has had very little impact from
human beings, it has an enormous heritage  value. These three island groups have
enjoyed World Heritage status, but, of co urse, as others have said, the waters
surrounding them do not enjoy that same status.
This is a bill that needs to protect the area of water around these islands. It is going to
be the first marine protected area to be implemented under our Government’s marine
protection areas policy. We were in Government when the Marines Reserve Act was
established back in 1971. That Act is no longe r fit for purpose. It is outdated and it
needs now to be improved upon. We need to have marine reserves that will have a

say, to marine protection.
World Heritage status does afford a lot of  protection, but protection of the marine
areas around the islands is a vital part of our overall  philosophy, which was outlined
very eloquently by the Minister of Conservation at the start of this debate tonight. The
very special ecology of these three islands is important to us. As the Minister said—and
I will leave it at this—the ocean environmen t is the new frontier for conservation. That
is why this bill, among the raft of meas ures that we are bringing in for marine
conservation, is so vital. I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Can I just begin by wishing you, Mr

There are some other areas , though, on which I think the Government and the
Minister of Conservation need to do a bit of  rethinking and recalibrating, and some of it

items.text: —and the board of inquiry process has not been able to give

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: The law says 9 months.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: That is how Ministers make instructions—through law. This

28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15587

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: Happy New Year to you, Mr Deputy Speaker. I

This piece of legislation is bringing in three new marine reserves. That will mean that

reserves, once these three new Subantarctic Islands reserves have been gazetted, and

This is the party that also introduced regulations covering the exclusive economic
zone. Other parties jump up and down, wail, and sound terrified at every proposal that
comes in, yet they were quite happy for a long time not to have any legislation operating
in the exclusive economic zone to regulate and protect our waters. We are the party that

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Is this a split call?

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: It is.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Phil Twyford—5 minutes.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: Labour is, of course, supporting the
Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill,  as my colleagues have pointed out. We
support the inclusion of these three areas in marine reserves. They are a treasure that
belongs to this country. They are part of th e World Heritage network, and it is the right
thing that they are included as part of the marine reserves. We congratulate the work of
the Minister of Conservation on getting the legislation to this point.
I want to make just a few comments about the general state of the marine reserves
legislation and note that this bill basically uses special legislation to achieve marine
reserve status for the Subantarctic Islands . The reserves are not being set up under the
law that currently exists for the creation of marine reserves, which is the Marine
Reserves Act 1971. That legislation, now 40 years old, is cumbersome. It was ahead of
its time when it was passed and highly rate d, but no longer. That legislation has been
left behind by international best  practice. Unfortunately, I thi nk, and in spite of the fact
that many New Zealanders applaud the goal of achieving 10 percent of our waters being
declared marine reserves, this has been a very difficult issue over the last couple of
decades.
I think the Minister would probably agree that that primary legislation is in dire need
of an overhaul. I think that most parties in this House would agree that work needs to be
done to find a mechanism that can work in th e kinds of political and social realities of
New Zealand conservation policy today. It wa s difficult, I think, during the time of the
28 Jan 2014 Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill  15589
last Labour Government when efforts were ma de to revamp that law and reform it. The
numbers in this House were not there. Ther e was not majority support to reform the
marine reserves legislation and update it. I hope that now there is majority support for
reforming that legislation, because it is long overdue.
The regulatory impact statement for this bill points out that the average time to
establish a marine reserve under the Marine Re serves Act is about 12 years. It ranges
between 1 and 23 years, and that clea rly is not good enough. The Environmental
Defence Society released a publication last year that I thought made some very good
points. It argued for the need to overhaul th e legislation and produce a Marine Reserves
Act that allows for the efficient promulgati on of marine reserves for the creation of a
network of different types of marine prot ected areas, all the way from no-take areas
right through to full protected reserves. I believe that we need that kind of legislation.
I spent much of last week kayaking around the Waitemat ā Harbour in the Hauraki
Gulf in Auckland, looking at conservation issues and talking to many of the movers and
shakers within the Hauraki Gulf Forum. That forum is a collaborative governance
model set up to advance the agenda of preserving the Hauraki Gulf for future
generations—cleaning it up, ad dressing issues of wate r quality, and protecting
biodiversity. The establishment of marine reserves—in fact, establishing the 10 percent
of the Hauraki Gulf earmarked as marine re serves—is one of the key elements in that
agenda, allowing crayfish, snapper, and other species to regenerate beyond current stock
levels so that the ecosystems can be rest ored and repaired and the gulf protected for
future generations.
Marine reserves are one of the really bi g challenges that we have. I hope that the
Hauraki Gulf Forum can achieve something like 10 percent of the Hauraki Gulf set
aside. It is a big ask and I hope that as we ll as establishing reformed marine reserve
legislation in this House we  actually see real, practical progress on the ground in places
like the Subantarctic Islands and places like the Hauraki Gulf. Thank you.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Happy New Year to you, Mr Deputy Speaker, and to
other members of this House and their fam ilies. I am pleased to take a call on the
Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves B ill, which, as Gareth Hughes explained, the
Green Party will be strongly supporting.
I congratulate the Minister of Conservation on  his stewardship of this bill, on getting
it to the House, and on his commitment to establishing a record number of marine
reserves this year. But we would also lik e to see progress on the marine reserves
legislation because, as Phil Twyford pointed out, it is outdated and it is cumbersome.
There have been a number of promises by Na tional and by the previous Minister of
Conservation to introduce a new marine rese rves bill. One has languished before the
select committee for over a decade and not progressed. Given that collaborative
processes are the flavour of the month now , we would like to se e some collaboration
around that legislation.
In a former life I was a member of the We st Coast Marine Protection Forum, which
made a number of recommendations to the Government on the reserves that are now
going to be established.  The reserves that conservation groups would have  liked to see
were somewhat larger than the ones that are being established, but that collaborative

where the common ground lay, to  understand others’ points of view, and to understand

Again, here in this bill, it is the result of a collaborative process and a forum that was
established to look at marine protection in the subantarctic. That is a process that was
triggered by the Marine Protected Areas Policy, which was introduced by the former
15590 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 28 Jan 2014
Labour Government, but there have been ve ry few of these collaborative forums
established under National until quite recen tly, when one was established, I think, in
Otago. They are a good process—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: And in Auckland.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Thank you, Minister—and in Auckla nd. With legislation that is
establishing protected areas and a review of the Marine Reserves Act, it would be
useful, I think, when we are de aling with law that is crea ting benefits for present and
future generations and that is  protecting biodiversity for its intrinsic values, that there
should not be the party politic al differences. We should be  able to establish common
ground. So it would be valuable, Minister, if  there was some discussion between parties
before the legislation was introduced to see whether and what sort of consensus could
be agreed on for the Marine Reserves Act, given that it failed before because of the
widespread different view s around it. So, Minister, we would encourage the
Government to look at similar consultation and a similar commitment to collaborative
processes before new legislation is introduced, and to that sort of collaboration that it is
endorsing at a regional level in investigating individual marine reserves.
Turning to this bill, we are pleased to s upport it. There is only one marine reserve in
the Subantarctic Islands at the moment, and that is around the Auckland Islands. That
was established in 2003. The islands are really important. They do have World Heritage
status because they are some of the least modified islands on the planet.
This bill is a step forward in giving us a marine reserve arou nd the Antipodes Island
and some protection around the Bounty Isla nds and Campbell Island. But—I do not
want to disappoint the Minist er—the Green Party believes th at the bill could go further
and could take on board the submissions by Environment and Conservation
Organisations of New Zealand, Forest and Bird, the Southland Conservation Board, and
others to protect the full extent of the territorial sea around the Bounty Islands and
around Campbell Island, because the very strange boundaries around those islands are
to ensure that the ling fishery continues a nd to allow for a speculative potential deep-
water crab fishery. There have  been investigatio ns in the 1970s and the 1990s of that
crab fishery. Nothing has come of it. Given the distance to the subantarctic and the cost
of diesel, it is unlikely to be profitable.
The Green Party would see a proper commitme nt to marine conservation and marine
protection by establishing the full extent of  the territorial sea around those islands as
marine reserves. That would recognise their internationally important values and World
Heritage status. Nevertheless, this bill is a step forward. Thank you.
